contentSections.answer: **The developer assigned the ticket — and only the findings they were assigned.** Nobody reads the whole document. The product owner reads the executive summary, legal reads the conformance section, procurement reads the scope. This is not a failure of your writing; it is what a reference document is for. Write each section to be readable alone, because that is how every section will be read.

contentSections.body:
The structure that serves all of them isn't complicated, and it isn't padding:

- **An executive summary of half a page.** What was tested, what wasn't, how bad it is, and the three things that matter most. This is the only part most readers will finish.
- **Findings, grouped by root cause rather than by page.** Forty instances of the same broken component is one finding with forty locations, not forty findings. The designer needs it grouped this way; the developer doesn't mind.
- **Each finding leading with task impact, then reproduction, then citation.** The order from lesson one, applied at the document level.
- **An explicit scope statement, including exclusions.** What you tested, on what, with what, and what you did not.

The temptation, especially early, is to demonstrate thoroughness by volume. A hundred-page report of undifferentiated findings reads as diligent and produces less change than a fifteen-page one with the same content grouped properly.

contentSections.scenario: An audit found the same broken custom dropdown component on 34 pages, plus four unrelated single-page defects.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that argues for reporting the dropdown as ONE finding with 34 locations rather than 34 findings.

items.label: The designer owns the component, not the 34 pages
It makes the total finding count look smaller
There is one fix, and it resolves all 34 at once
Rating it once avoids 34 separate severity arguments
It avoids alarming the client with the real scale
Retesting is one verification instead of 34

explanation.designer: The strongest reason. Grouping by root cause is what makes an audit legible to the person who can prevent the whole class recurring.
explanation.count: A worse-looking number is not a reason to restructure a report, and a reader who notices you did it will distrust everything else. Group because it reflects the causal structure, not because it flatters the total.
explanation.fix: One change to one component. Thirty-four tickets would be thirty-four people discovering that.
explanation.severity: Severity attaches to the barrier, and it is the same barrier every time. Rating it 34 times invites 34 chances to rate it inconsistently.
explanation.hide: The opposite of the goal. The grouped finding must state all 34 locations explicitly — the scale is the evidence for prioritising it.
explanation.retest: And it means the retest can be honest: verified once, on the component, rather than sampled across pages.

contentSections.synthesis: Group by cause, list every instance. The two are not in tension — a single finding with 34 named locations tells the designer what to fix, the developer where to check, and the product owner exactly how big it is. Thirty-four findings tell all three of them less.

contentSections.body: Group by root cause, lead every finding with task impact, and put the scope — including what you didn't test — where nobody can miss it.

contentSections.title: Where the decision actually gets made

contentSections.body: Most accessibility work is decided by someone who will never read a finding: a buyer choosing between two suppliers, months before anything is built.

contentSections.scenario: A university is procuring a student records system. Three vendors bid. All three supply an accessibility conformance statement claiming WCAG 2.1 AA. The university buys the cheapest. Two years later, disabled students cannot use it, and the university has no leverage — the contract is signed and the vendor's position is that the statement was accurate at the time.
contentSections.question: Where was this outcome actually decided?

options.label: At procurement, when nobody checked the statements against evidence
In the vendor's development team, when they cut accessibility work
When the university failed to audit after go-live

feedback.procurement: Right. Three unverified claims were treated as three equivalent facts, so the only remaining differentiator was price. Everything after that follows.
feedback.vendor: The vendor's choices produced the defects, but the university's process created the incentive: if an unverified claim is worth the same as a verified one, there is no commercial reason to do the work.
feedback.audit: A post-go-live audit would have documented the problem and provided no remedy. The contract was already signed, with no accessibility obligations that survive it.

contentSections.mechanism:
The mechanism is **an unverified claim being priced the same as a verified one.** Accessibility statements are self-declared. Where nobody asks for evidence behind them, they carry no information, and a procurement process that treats them as equivalent selects on price alone — which systematically rewards the vendor that did the least.

The intervention is upstream of everything an auditor normally does: ask for the audit that backs the statement, ask who performed it and when, ask what was in scope, and put remediation obligations in the contract. That is a twenty-minute change to a procurement checklist, and it is worth more than most audits.

contentSections.body:
This is why accessibility statements are worth reading adversarially, and why an audit's scope section is the part with real consequences. Your report may end up as the evidence behind a statement that a buyer relies on.

So: never let a scope section imply more coverage than you delivered. "WCAG 2.1 AA audit of the customer portal" and "WCAG 2.1 AA audit of five journeys within the customer portal, listed below, on the browser and assistive technology combinations listed below" are different claims, and the difference is the whole value of the document.

contentSections.question: You audited five journeys out of a forty-page portal and found them broadly sound. The client's draft accessibility statement says "this service conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA." What do you tell them?
contentSections.hint: What would your audit actually support, if a procurement reviewer asked you directly?
contentSections.answer:
That the statement claims more than your audit evidences, and that they should say what was tested. A defensible version: *"Five core journeys, listed below, were independently audited against WCAG 2.1 AA in March 2026 and found to conform. The remainder of the service has not been independently assessed."*

That is a weaker-sounding sentence and a much stronger position. The first version is the one that becomes a problem when a disabled user cannot use page thirty-seven.

contentSections.body: The biggest accessibility decisions get made at procurement by people who never read a finding. Write the scope section as if it will be quoted, because it might be.

title: Doing This Work at Variable Capacity
description: Structuring an audit into stages that survive being interrupted, keeping evidence you can return to cold, and renegotiating scope without either over-explaining or over-promising.

learningObjectives.text: Stage an audit so any stage boundary is a safe stopping point
Keep evidence that lets you resume work cold after days away
Renegotiate scope by offering a costed choice rather than an apology

contentSections.title: Auditing in stages that can be interrupted

contentSections.body: The reason to structure an audit into resumable stages is not that you might have a bad week. It's that you will, and an audit structured as one long push turns that into a client conversation instead of a Tuesday.

contentSections.question: Put these audit stages in the order that leaves the most usable partial result if you have to stop after any one of them.
steps: Scope: list the journeys, pages, browsers and assistive technology combinations you will cover — and the ones you won't
Automated pass across the full scope, with results triaged into confirmed, dismissed and needs-checking
Keyboard-only pass through each journey, recording where each one stops
Screen reader pass through each journey, recording announcements verbatim
Severity rating and grouping of every finding by root cause
Report writing: executive summary, findings, scope statement
contentSections.explanation:
The property that matters is that **every boundary is a defensible stopping point**. Stop after stage one and the client has a scope they can hand to someone else. Stop after three and they have real, actionable keyboard findings. Stop after five and they have a prioritised backlog even without the prose.

The common alternative — working journey by journey, doing all methods on each before moving on — feels more natural and fails badly on interruption: you end up with journey one exhaustively covered and journeys two through five untouched, which is much harder to hand over and much easier to mistake for full coverage.

The keyboard pass sits before the screen reader pass deliberately. It's less demanding, it finds a large share of the barriers, and it means a low-capacity day still moves the audit forward.

contentSections.body:
Two more habits that make interruption survivable:

**Batch by access method, not by page.** Every switch between keyboard-only and screen reader review costs real setup and real mental reorientation. Doing all the keyboard work, then all the screen reader work, cuts that cost to two transitions for the whole audit.

**Write the finding when you see it, not later.** A note that says *"checkout — something odd with the date picker"* is worthless in four days. Ninety seconds spent capturing the task, the access method, where it stopped and the environment is the difference between resuming and re-doing.

contentSections.scenario: You stop mid-audit having written eleven findings as terse personal notes — the kind that make complete sense while the page is still open in front of you. You come back six days later.
contentSections.question: Of those eleven, how many will you be able to write up properly without re-testing the page?
contentSections.explanation:
The specific number varies; the shape doesn't. What survives is whatever you captured explicitly — and terse notes capture the *observation* while silently relying on context that has evaporated: which browser, which page state, what you had done immediately before, what exactly was announced.

The practical consequence is that re-testing eight findings costs far more than the fifteen minutes writing them properly would have. This is the single highest-return habit in the job for anyone whose working days are not guaranteed, and it is worth building before you need it rather than after the week you lose.

contentSections.body: Stage by method, not by page, so every boundary is a stopping point — and write each finding at the moment you see it.

At some point you will have to tell a client you cannot deliver what you agreed. The instinct is to explain your health. Resist it: the client cannot act on your symptoms, and it moves the conversation somewhere neither of you wants it.

contentSections.scenario:
Three ways of telling a client the same thing.

**A.** *"I've had a flare-up of my condition and have been unable to work since Tuesday. I'm so sorry — I know this is frustrating. I'll do everything I can to catch up and hopefully still deliver on time."*

**B.** *"Running slightly behind, will update you Friday."*

**C.** *"I've lost four working days against nine days of scoped work. Two options, with what each costs you — I'd recommend the first. Let me know by Thursday and I'll re-scope accordingly."*
contentSections.question: Which of these puts the client in a position to make a decision?

options.label: A — it's honest and gives the full context
B — it's brief and doesn't over-share
C — it names the gap and offers costed options

feedback.a: It is honest, and honesty isn't the problem. The problem is that it hands the client medical information they cannot act on, a promise you may not be able to keep — *hopefully still deliver on time* — and no decision to make. It also invites them to manage your health, which is not a relationship you want.
feedback.b: Brief is good and the instinct to not over-share is right, but this defers the problem without shrinking it. The client still thinks nine days of work is coming, and on Friday you will have the same conversation with less time left to act on it.
feedback.c: Yes. It states the gap as a fact, offers a real choice, prices each option, and gives a decision deadline. It contains no medical information at all, and it doesn't need any: the client's problem is the delivery, and that is what you've addressed.

contentSections.concept:
**State the gap, offer costed options, recommend one, set a decision deadline.** No diagnosis, no apology beyond a sentence, no promise that depends on your body cooperating.

This is not about concealment. It's that a client needs a decision, and your health is not a variable they can adjust. Give them what they can act on. If your capacity is genuinely variable in a way that affects how you should be engaged, that's a conversation to have at scoping — in terms of working pattern and buffers, not in terms of symptoms.

contentSections.body: State the gap, price the options, recommend one, set a deadline. Your diagnosis is not a project variable.

title: Practice — Findings, Methods and Readers
description: Eight drills on the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where recognising a barrier stops being something you have read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the finding procedure to unfamiliar observations at speed
Classify barriers by detection method and by whether a criterion covers them

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or three — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write Your Own Reviewer Profile
description: Produce the document that states which assistive technology you can review with authority, where you need a co-reviewer, and what you will write into a scope section as a result.

learningObjectives.text: Assess your own reviewing authority honestly across access needs
Produce a reviewer profile a client could rely on

contentSections.body: Every professional reviewer has a document like this, whether or not they've written it down. Writing it down is what turns "I'm not sure I can judge that" from a moment of doubt mid-audit into a line in your scope section that makes you look like you know what you're doing — because you do.

contentSections.title: Your reviewer profile
contentSections.brief:
A prospective client asks: *"What can you actually review, and what would you need help with?"*

This is a completely reasonable question and most reviewers answer it badly — either by over-claiming ("I can audit against WCAG 2.1 AA", which says nothing about method) or by under-claiming (hedging everything because they're early in their career).

Write the document you'd send. It is for a client, so it is short, specific and free of apology.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-page reviewer profile: what you can review with authority, what you review against guidance, what needs a co-reviewer or user testing, and the scope wording that follows from it.

stages.title: Inventory what you actually use
stages.instructions:
List every access method you use or have used: screen reader (which, how long, how fluently), magnification, keyboard-only, voice control, switch, reduced motion, anything else. Be honest about level — "NVDA, six years, navigate by heading and landmark" is a different claim from "NVDA, three months, mostly tabbing."

Include nothing you haven't used. This is not a skills list to pad.
stages.checkpoint: You have a list where every entry names the technology, the duration, and how you actually navigate with it.

stages.title: Sort your review authority into three tiers
stages.instructions:
Using the three-way split from lesson three, sort what you can review into:

**Direct authority** — you use this daily and can write findings from your own use as evidence.
**Against guidance** — you can review it competently using standards, tooling and technique, but you are not the user.
**Needs a co-reviewer or user testing** — you can flag concerns but cannot settle them.

Every access need in WCAG should land in one of the three. Resist putting things in tier one because you'd like them there.
stages.checkpoint: Every major access need appears in exactly one tier, and you could defend each placement out loud.

stages.title: Write the blind-spot section
stages.instructions:
Add a short section naming the two failure modes from lesson three that apply to you specifically:

- Which barriers have you learned to work around so fluently that you might not register them as barriers?
- Which access needs would you be at risk of judging by your own standard rather than the user's?

One or two sentences each. This section is the one that will make a good client trust you.
stages.checkpoint: You have named at least two concrete blind spots, not generic humility.

stages.title: Turn it into scope wording
stages.instructions:
Write the two or three sentences you would paste into an audit scope section. They should state which methods the audit covers, which assistive technology and version, and — explicitly — what was not tested and why.

Write it as a claim you'd be comfortable seeing quoted by a procurement reviewer two years later, because lesson four is about exactly that happening.
stages.checkpoint: The wording states coverage and exclusions, and contains no claim you couldn't evidence.

stages.title: Cut it to one page and self-check
stages.instructions:
Cut it to a page. Then read it as the client: would you hire this person? Would you know what you were getting? Is there any sentence that is apologising rather than informing?

Then run the self-check below against your own draft.
stages.checkpoint: It fits on one page, and every sentence either informs a decision or is gone.

rubric.criterion: Every claim is specific enough to check
rubric.meets: Technology is named with version or duration of use; "experienced with screen readers" has been replaced with something a client could verify.

rubric.criterion: The three tiers are genuinely distinguished
rubric.meets: Nothing sits in direct-authority that you couldn't write a finding about from your own use, and the needs-help tier is not empty.

rubric.criterion: Blind spots are concrete
rubric.meets: Names specific barriers or access needs, not a general statement of humility. A reader learns something they couldn't have guessed.

rubric.criterion: The scope wording states exclusions
rubric.meets: Says what was not tested, plainly, in a sentence that would survive being quoted by someone comparing suppliers.

rubric.criterion: It reads as professional, not apologetic
rubric.meets: No sentence apologises for a limitation. Limitations are stated as method, which is what they are.

rubric.criterion: It fits on one page
rubric.meets: A client can read the whole thing in two minutes and know what they'd be getting.

contentSections.body: Knowing the edge of your own authority, and writing it down before anyone asks, is the difference between a reviewer and someone who reviews.

title: Checkpoint — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
description: Ten questions pulling across the module. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — What Accessibility QA Actually Is

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a violation and a barrier?

options.label: A violation breaks a criterion; a barrier stops a task
A violation is Level A; a barrier is Level AA
They're the same thing described from two perspectives

questions.explanation: They overlap and neither contains the other. There are violations that block nobody and blockers no criterion cleanly names — and the second group is the one that gets argued with, so it needs the most careful writing.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: In the finding procedure, what comes first?

options.label: The success criterion
The task the user was trying to complete
The reproduction steps

questions.explanation: Task, access method, where it stops, what they're left with, citation. Starting from the criterion produces audits that are technically complete and impossible to prioritise.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Roughly what share of accessibility barriers does an automated scanner detect on a typical site?

options.label: About 30%, though the figure depends heavily on how you count
About 70%
Nearly all of them, if configured well

questions.explanation: Somewhere in the 20–40% range. But the more useful fact is *which* share: scanners are near-complete on markup properties and structurally blind to meaning, layout and runtime behaviour.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Which of these can a scanner reliably detect?

options.label: alt="product image" on 40 different products
A <label> whose for attribute points at a nonexistent id
Focus never moving into a modal when it opens

questions.explanation: A broken for/id reference is a pure markup property. The other two need, respectively, knowing what the images show and observing runtime behaviour.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: How does a fluent screen reader user usually navigate an unfamiliar page?

options.label: Tabbing through in DOM order
Jumping by heading and landmark, then reading forward
Reading the whole page from the top

questions.explanation: Tab is the slow fallback, reached for last. Which is why a review conducted by tabbing exercises the fallback path and misses every failure in the structural path a fluent user actually uses.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: What does expertise with an assistive technology do to your reviewing?

options.label: Makes you better at everything
Makes you better in your lane and can blind you to barriers you've learned to route around
Disqualifies you from objectivity

questions.explanation: Every barrier you've learned to work around is one you may stop registering as a barrier — and those are systematically the ones affecting people newer to the technology, which is a very large group.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: A product owner reads the audit first. What do they need first?

options.label: The criterion and conformance level
Which user journey is blocked and for whom
Reproduction steps

questions.explanation: Five readers, five first questions. The product owner is ranking a backlog, so they need impact. The developer needs reproduction; legal needs exposure; procurement needs the scope statement.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Why do accessibility statements matter so much at procurement?

options.label: They're legally binding contracts
They're self-declared, so unverified claims get priced the same as verified ones
They're produced by independent auditors

questions.explanation: Which means the only remaining differentiator is price, which systematically rewards whoever did least. Asking for the audit behind the statement is a twenty-minute change to a checklist worth more than most audits.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Why stage an audit by access method rather than journey by journey?

options.label: It's faster overall
Every stage boundary becomes a defensible stopping point
Clients prefer the report structure

questions.explanation: Stop after the keyboard pass and the client has real, actionable findings across the whole scope. Journey-by-journey leaves you with one journey covered exhaustively and the rest untouched — harder to hand over and easy to mistake for coverage.

questions.from: This module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: What belongs in the message when you can't deliver the scope you agreed?

options.label: An explanation of what happened medically
The gap, costed options, a recommendation, and a decision deadline
A brief note that you're running behind, with a fuller update later

questions.explanation: The client needs a decision. Your diagnosis is not a variable they can adjust, and deferring the conversation just shrinks the time available to act on it.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Impairment, Barrier, Disability: Three Different Words
description: Why the medical model locates the problem in the wrong place, what the social model changes about that, and how to rewrite a finding so it names the barrier instead of the person.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish impairment, barrier and disability as three separate things
Locate the cause of a specific access failure in the design rather than the person
Rewrite deficit-framed language as barrier-framed language

contentSections.body:
A woman using a wheelchair arrives at a conference venue. Three steps lead up to the entrance. No ramp, no lift, no alternative route. The event programme later describes the day as "accessible, with one small barrier for wheelchair users."

Read that sentence again. The entrance failed to let her in. The sentence files the failure under her, not under the three steps someone poured in concrete.

contentSections.scenario: Same venue. The steps were built in 1974, before an accessibility requirement existed for that building class. Nobody currently working there designed them. A staff member says: "It's not really anyone's fault — she just can't manage stairs."
contentSections.question: What is actually broken here?

options.label: Her body, which cannot climb stairs
The entrance, which was designed with only one route in
Both, equally — it takes two things to make a barrier

feedback.entrance: Yes. Her mobility is a fact about her body — real, and not something this lesson is trying to talk her out of. The barrier is a separate fact: this building was designed with exactly one way in, and that way requires a kind of movement not everyone has. Nobody currently on staff built the steps. The steps are still, today, the thing stopping her — not her wheelchair.
feedback.body: This is the medical-model reflex: the problem gets located in the person, because the person is the visible variable in the room. Her wheelchair works fine on flat ground, in a lift, on a ramp. It only "fails" against a specific design choice — stairs — that could have been built differently for the same cost, in 1974 or since.
feedback.both: It's tempting to split the difference, but notice what that framing does: it makes the fix optional, a shared burden between a building and a body, rather than a design failure with a design fix. Nothing about her body has to change for this barrier to disappear. A ramp does that on its own.

contentSections.concept:
**The medical model** treats disability as a deficit located in a person, to be diagnosed, minimised or worked around by the individual. **The social model** treats disability as the outcome of an environment designed without a person's needs in mind — the problem sits in the design, and the fix is a design fix.

This course uses the social model as a working tool, not as a denial that impairments are real and sometimes limiting on their own terms (chronic pain is still pain, with or without a barrier attached). The claim is narrower and more useful for this job: **when you find yourself describing an access failure as something wrong with the user, check whether you've actually found something wrong with the design.**

contentSections.body:
It's worth being precise about the three words, because the whole vocabulary of this course rests on the distinction:

- **Impairment** — a fact about a body or mind: low vision, chronic pain, dyslexia, deafness, a tremor. Real, and not itself the target of your work.
- **Barrier** — a fact about a design: low-contrast text, a video with no captions, a form with no error recovery, three steps and no ramp. This is the target of your work.
- **Disability** — what happens when the two meet. Not fixed, not permanent, not solely a property of the person: the same impairment produces disability against one barrier and nothing against another.

The reason this distinction earns a whole lesson: an audit that reports on impairments ("this page is hard for blind users") produces nothing actionable. An audit that reports on barriers ("this image has no alt text, so a screen reader announces the filename instead of the content") produces a ticket a developer can close.

contentSections.code:
Bug report #482

Blind users are limited in what they can do on the
product page — they can't tell which variant (colour,
size) they're selecting because the swatches don't
announce anything. Recommend training content team
to be more accessibility-aware.
contentSections.question: This report has a real observation buried in it. What's the flaw in how it's written?

options.label: It should say "visually impaired" instead of "blind"
It locates the problem in blind users instead of in the unlabelled swatches
It doesn't cite a WCAG success criterion

feedback.location: Correct. "Blind users are limited" puts the deficit on the user. The actual defect is a design fact: colour swatches implemented as `<div>` elements with a background-color and no text alternative, so nothing is exposed to the accessibility tree. Fix the swatches — every blind user of this page benefits, and the recommendation ("train the content team") doesn't even point at the right team, because this is a markup defect, not a content one.
feedback.wording: Word choice matters less than it looks here — "blind" is a perfectly acceptable term many blind people use for themselves. The report's real problem survives any wording fix: it still doesn't say what's wrong with the page.
feedback.citation: A citation would help (1.1.1 Non-text Content, or 4.1.2 if the swatches need a role too), but adding one to a report that still blames the user for the swatches' failure doesn't fix the report. Fix the location of the problem first.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The tell is the recommendation: "train the content team to be more accessibility-aware" is not a fix for anything, because the bug isn't a content problem. When a finding is framed around what users can't do rather than what the design fails to provide, the recommended fix drifts toward vague sensitivity training instead of a specific code change — `aria-label` on each swatch, or a visually-hidden text node naming the colour. Barrier-framing doesn't just read better. It routes the ticket to the right place.

contentSections.body: Impairment is a fact about a body. Barrier is a fact about a design. Disability is what happens when they meet — and only one of those three is yours to fix.

A teammate says, in a planning meeting: "We can't make this fully accessible — some users are just too impaired to use a computer at all." Nobody in the room disagrees. This lesson is about the assumption that sentence is quietly making.

contentSections.scenario: The same low-vision user from above is now reviewing a third product: a hospital patient portal. Below are six statements people on the project have said about her experience of it.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that correctly locates the disability in the barrier rather than in her impairment.

items.label: "She can't read the discharge summary because it's 11px grey text on white."
"She's too visually impaired to use the portal."
"The portal's default zoom breaks at 150%, well below what she needs."
"Low-vision users generally struggle with hospital software."
"At 200% zoom with the browser's own reader mode, she reads it fine — the portal's own styling is what breaks first."
"She just needs to ask a family member to read it to her."

explanation.s1: Names the design property (11px, insufficient contrast) that causes the failure. Fixable, specific, assigns the work to the right place.
explanation.s2: Restates her impairment as if it were sufficient explanation on its own, with no design fact attached. It also generalises from one product to her as a category.
explanation.s3: Same shape as s1 — a measurable design property (the breakpoint) that a developer can locate and change.
explanation.s4: A generalisation about a whole group with no product fact in it at all. Useless for a report and quietly implies the barrier is inherent to "hospital software" rather than to this portal's specific styling.
explanation.s5: The strongest of the six: it isolates exactly what's failing (the portal's own CSS) by showing what happens when that specific layer is removed. This is the kind of observation that turns into a precise finding.
explanation.s6: Treats the barrier as permanent and routes around it through another person's unpaid labour, instead of naming what a fix would look like. Also not something an audit gets to recommend — it isn't a fix, it's a workaround that shouldn't be necessary.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six name a design property. Three describe the same situation as if it were a fact about her. Notice that the useful three are also, not coincidentally, the ones a developer could act on without knowing anything else about her — which is the actual test for whether a statement has located the barrier correctly.

contentSections.body:
Take one person with one impairment — low vision, say, corrected to a level where large print and good contrast let her read comfortably. Put her in front of two dashboards.

**Dashboard A** has body text at 16px, a contrast ratio of 7:1, and supports 200% browser zoom without breaking the layout. She uses it without incident.

**Dashboard B** has body text at 11px in `#999` on white — a contrast ratio of 2.85:1 — and the layout breaks into overlapping columns above 150% zoom. She cannot read it.

Her impairment did not change between the two products. What changed is the barrier. She is disabled by Dashboard B and not by Dashboard A — and that sentence only makes grammatical sense once you stop treating "disability" as a fixed label stuck to a person and start treating it as a relationship between a person and a specific design.
Same impairment, different barriers, different disability. That's the whole model — and it's the reason accessibility work is design work, not charity.

title: The Range of Access Needs One Product Has to Serve
description: The major categories of access need a product meets at once, why they overlap and sometimes pull against each other, and why 'we made it accessible' rarely means what the team think it means.

learningObjectives.text: Enumerate the major categories of access need a product has to serve simultaneously
Recognise when a single accessibility fix addresses only one category and leaves others untouched
Resolve a case where two access needs pull a design decision in different directions

contentSections.body: A team redesigns a checkout flow "for accessibility." The one change that ships is larger buttons. Three weeks later, a support ticket arrives from a screen reader user who still cannot complete checkout — the buttons were never the thing stopping her. The team didn't lie. They made one real improvement and quietly treated accessibility as one thing to fix rather than several.

A product that reaches a broad user base has to serve, at minimum, all of these at once — and this list is not exhaustive:

- **Vision** — blindness, low vision, colour vision deficiency
- **Hearing** — deafness, hard of hearing
- **Mobility and motor** — limited dexterity, tremor, one-handed use, no reliable pointing device
- **Cognitive** — memory load, attention, processing speed, dyslexia, intellectual disability
- **Speech** — for anything relying on voice input
- **Variable and fluctuating capacity** — chronic illness, fatigue, pain, brain fog that changes day to day

Bigger buttons help the motor category and can actively hurt the cognitive one if they eat the space a clear layout needs. Nothing in this list is a small minority stacked at the edge of a bell curve: government disability statistics in most countries with reliable data put the working-age share at roughly one in four, and that's before counting the situational and temporary needs the next lesson covers.

contentSections.scenario: You're briefing a product team who assume accessibility work serves "a small number of edge-case users." You want a number to open with.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of working-age adults in the UK report a disability under the Equality Act's definition?
contentSections.explanation: Government statistics put it at roughly one in five working-age adults — and that figure counts only people who meet a specific legal threshold (a condition with a substantial, long-term effect on ability to do normal daily activities), which excludes most situational and temporary access needs and undercounts conditions people don't disclose. Whatever the exact figure in your market, the honest framing for a briefing is: this is not an edge case. It is a substantial, continuous share of anyone's user base, present in every single release.

contentSections.body: A product serves several access categories at once, not one. "We fixed accessibility" almost always means "we fixed one category of it."

contentSections.title: When two needs pull in different directions

contentSections.body: Big touch targets help a tremor. Big touch targets also eat the screen space a magnification user needs to see more than one field at a time. Two real access needs, pulling the same control in opposite directions — and neither one is wrong to have.

contentSections.scenario:
A mobile form has two competing proposals in review. Proposal A: 56px touch targets with generous spacing, following WCAG 2.5.8's Level AAA minimum. Proposal B: 44px targets (the Level AA minimum) with denser layout, so all seven fields fit on screen without scrolling.

A reviewer says: "There's no accessible answer here — every option fails someone."
contentSections.question: Is the reviewer right that there's no accessible answer?

options.label: Yes — any target size choice will exclude someone, so the decision is arbitrary
No — one option is closer to a hard block for someone, and that should decide it
No — accessibility standards give one objectively correct size, end of discussion

feedback.hardblock: Right. A smaller target that's still tappable is friction for a tremor — real, worth minimising, but survivable with a retry. A layout that forces scrolling and re-orientation on every field is a much larger cost for someone at 400% zoom, who has already lost most of their spatial context. When two access needs genuinely pull against each other, the tie-break is which failure mode is closer to "cannot complete the task at all" versus "costs extra effort." Here that points at protecting the zoom user's layout and accepting the smaller — but still AA-compliant — target size, with generous spacing to reduce mis-taps.
feedback.arbitrary: This is the reflex that makes teams give up on the decision entirely and ship whatever's easiest. It isn't true that every choice is equally bad — one of these two costs someone a completed task, and the other costs someone a bit more precision. Those are not the same size of harm.
feedback.onesize: 56px would be preferable in isolation, but a decision made without the layout consequence for the zoom user isn't complete — a standard's minimum doesn't resolve a trade-off between two different standards' worth of needs pulling on the same layout.

contentSections.mechanism: This is what a genuine trade-off looks like, and it's worth naming as one rather than pretending an obvious answer exists. The job isn't to find the design that satisfies everyone identically — that design frequently doesn't exist. The job is to identify, specifically, what each option costs which group, and to weight task-blocking failures above friction. Writing that reasoning down, in the finding or the design decision log, is what separates a considered trade-off from an accidental one nobody chose on purpose.

contentSections.body: When two access needs genuinely conflict, the tie-break is which failure blocks a task outright versus which one just adds friction — and the reasoning belongs in writing, not left implicit.

title: Situational, Temporary and Fluctuating Access Needs
description: Why the same caption serves a Deaf colleague, a commuter with a muted phone and someone with a bad office speaker — and why fluctuating capacity is a distinct category from both, with its own design requirements.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish permanent, temporary, situational and fluctuating access needs
Identify a design's assumption that access needs are static
Specify a minimal fix for a barrier that specifically fails fluctuating capacity

contentSections.body: Someone captions a training video for a Deaf colleague. That same caption is what lets a second colleague follow it muted on a train, and what lets a third one read along because the office kitchen's ceiling speaker mangles half the consonants. One caption. Three completely different reasons somebody needed it, only one of which is permanent.

contentSections.scenario: A product backlog has a ticket: "Add captions — Deaf user requested it." A reviewer flags the ticket description as too narrow.
contentSections.question: Who does the finished caption barrier actually affect, once it ships?

options.label: Only Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, as scoped
A much wider range, including situational and temporary needs the ticket didn't name
Nobody but the person who requested it — captions are a personalisation feature

feedback.wide: Correct, and this is the whole reason the framework in this lesson matters: the same fix serves people whose need is permanent (Deaf, hard of hearing), people whose need is situational (open-plan office, muted phone on a train, a noisy warehouse), and people whose need is temporary (an ear infection, a burst eardrum recovering). None of them show up in a ticket scoped to a single requester's permanent need — and scoping it that narrowly risks the fix being deprioritised as "one person's accommodation" instead of recognised as broad-reach work.
feedback.narrow: This is the scoping mistake the ticket made, and it undersells the fix badly — captions are one of the highest-reach accessibility features that exist precisely because they serve every one of the four categories in this lesson at once.
feedback.personal: Captions aren't a preference toggle for one person's taste; they're a text alternative for audio content, which is exactly the kind of barrier this whole module is about — a design property, not an individual accommodation.

contentSections.concept:
**The permanent / temporary / situational / fluctuating framework** (adapted from Microsoft's inclusive design research) separates access needs by how long they last and where they come from:

- **Permanent** — a lasting characteristic: blind, one arm, Deaf.
- **Temporary** — resolves and doesn't come back: an eye infection, a broken arm in a cast, a burst eardrum.
- **Situational** — caused by the environment, not the body: bright sunlight on a phone screen, a noisy warehouse, holding a baby in one arm.
- **Fluctuating** — internal, unpredictable and recurring, covered in the next section — the category this course's audience knows from the inside.

The same barrier — no captions, low contrast, a tiny tap target — can land on someone in any of the four categories. Designing only for the permanent case is common, and it's the reason accessibility work quietly under-serves a much larger population than the one it explicitly named.

contentSections.body:
One axis, worked through concretely for vision:

| Category | Example |
|---|---|
| Permanent | Blindness |
| Temporary | Recovering from eye surgery, dilated pupils after an exam |
| Situational | Direct sunlight washing out a phone screen |
| Fluctuating | Migraine aura, or a chronic condition whose visual symptoms come and go |

Every row needs roughly the same design property to work — sufficient contrast, text that isn't locked to a fixed size, content that doesn't depend on colour alone. Which is the practical upshot: designing well for the permanent case usually covers the other three for free. Designing *only* against the permanent case as an explicit checklist item, while dismissing the rest as "not really disabled," is how a team convinces itself a fix is niche when it is actually broad.

contentSections.scenario: A product team is deciding which access needs "count" for a sprint's accessibility work. Six people and their circumstances are on the table.
contentSections.question: Select every person who has a genuine access need right now — someone for whom the interface, as built, either helps or actively fails them in this moment.

items.label: Someone reading a bright screen outdoors at midday, glare washing out low-contrast text
Someone with a sprained wrist in a splint, typing one-handed for six weeks
Someone with congenital low vision using a screen magnifier every day of their life
Someone holding a sleeping toddler, navigating one-handed with their thumb
Someone with well-managed, fully corrected short-sightedness wearing their glasses as usual
Someone with a chronic pain condition whose grip strength varies day to day, using a mouse today when it flares

explanation.p1: Situational — the barrier is entirely environmental (glare), not a property of this person's vision, and it will resolve the moment they go indoors.
explanation.p2: Temporary — real, time-bound, and typically undercounted because a splint is visible and treated as self-evidently temporary rather than as an access need with the same design requirements as any motor impairment.
explanation.p3: Permanent — the category most designs at least attempt to serve, though often badly.
explanation.p4: Situational, and one of the clearest examples: nothing about their body has changed, and the barrier (needing one-handed operation) is entirely produced by circumstance.
explanation.p5: Not currently a live access need — corrected vision with glasses on is the case a product doesn't need to design around specifically, which is worth including precisely because it's the baseline everything else is being compared against.
explanation.p6: Fluctuating — the defining feature is that it varies, unpredictably, for the same person across days, and the interface has to work on the bad days as well as the good ones.

contentSections.synthesis: Five of the six have a live access need in this exact moment, and only one of the five is permanent. A design reviewed only against "does this work for a blind user and a Deaf user" — the two most commonly checked permanent categories — has said nothing about the other four people on this list, all of whom are real and all of whom are common.

contentSections.body: Permanent, temporary, situational, fluctuating — one barrier, four different routes to the same failure. Design for the permanent case properly and the other three are usually covered for free.

contentSections.title: Fluctuating: not a phase, a pattern

contentSections.body: Someone with a fluctuating condition — POTS, ME/CFS, migraine, a relapsing-remitting illness — completes a benefits form in eight minutes on a good day. On a bad day, the same person, the same interface, cannot finish it at all. A form that only works on good days doesn't work.

contentSections.problem: A multi-page government benefits application times out after 20 minutes of inactivity, with no warning and no save. A caseworker reports that applicants with fluctuating conditions abandon it disproportionately. Diagnose the access need this fails, and specify a minimal fix.

steps.label: Name the access need affected
steps.work: Fluctuating capacity — specifically, the requirement that the whole form be completed within a single continuous, unpredictable session length.
steps.why: Naming the category correctly points at the right fix. This isn't a cognitive-load problem (the form itself may be perfectly clear) or a motor problem — it's a session-design problem that specifically punishes anyone whose available minutes aren't guaranteed.

steps.label: State the observed failure precisely
steps.work: 20-minute idle timeout, no warning before it fires, no autosave, no way to resume a partially completed application.
steps.why: Each of those four facts is independently fixable, and naming all four means the fix doesn't stop at the first one found.

steps.label: State what's lost when it fails
steps.work: Every field entered up to that point — for a benefits form, this can include sensitive information re-entered from memory, and re-entering it is itself a task cost, not a neutral inconvenience.
steps.why: This is the severity argument. "Loses data" undersells it; "loses twenty minutes of disclosure about your own medical history, with no guarantee you can gather the energy to redo it today" is what actually happened to the caseworker's clients.

steps.label: Specify the minimal fix
steps.work: Autosave on every field blur (not just on a timer), a generous or removable timeout with a warning and one-click extension, and a resume link emailed or saved to the account so the applicant can return days later without starting over.
steps.why: Minimal means: does not require rebuilding the form, does not require a new backend, and directly reverses each of the three named failures — no scope creep into a redesign.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. An online grocery checkout requires the entire order — browsing, cart, address, payment — to be completed in one browser session; closing the tab loses the cart. A customer with chronic fatigue reports having to "restart from nothing" three times before finishing one order.

blanks.why: Same category as the worked case — an unpredictable, recurring need for the task to survive an interruption.

blanks.prompt: State the observed failure in one clause.
blanks.answer: the cart is lost when the session or tab closes
blanks.why: Precise enough that a developer knows exactly what state needs to survive: the cart contents, tied to the account rather than the browser tab.

blanks.prompt: What does the customer lose each time it fails?
blanks.answer: everything they had added to the cart
blanks.why: For someone assembling an order in short bursts across a bad week, this is not a minor annoyance — it can mean giving up on the order entirely rather than repeating the browsing effort a fourth time.

blanks.prompt: Specify the minimal fix in one sentence.
blanks.answer: persist the cart to the account so it survives closing the tab or browser
accept: save the cart server-side, tied to the logged-in account
make the cart persistent across sessions
blanks.why: This is the smallest change that reverses the failure — no redesign of checkout, just moving cart state from the session to the account.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the access need → state the failure precisely → state what's lost → specify the minimal fix.** The same shape as the finding procedure from the previous module, applied specifically to fluctuating capacity: the fix is almost always about state surviving an interruption, because the interruption itself is the one variable this population cannot control.

contentSections.body:
Fluctuating access needs are distinct from temporary ones in a way worth being precise about: temporary resolves and stays resolved — the cast comes off and the wrist heals. Fluctuating recurs, unpredictably, indefinitely: the bad day comes back, on no fixed schedule, and the person cannot plan around it in advance.

What this means concretely for design:

- **No punishing timeouts.** A session that expires after fifteen idle minutes assumes the user can always keep moving. Someone who has to stop mid-task and lie down cannot.
- **Save state, always.** Losing entered data to a timeout or a crash isn't an inconvenience for this population — it can be the difference between finishing a task this month or not at all.
- **No forced single-sitting completion.** A form that must be done in one pass, with no way to save and return, quietly excludes anyone whose capacity doesn't hold for the whole thing.
- **Works one-handed, lying down, on a phone.** Not a nice-to-have posture — the actual posture a meaningful share of users are in.

This is also, not incidentally, the entire reason this track's own architecture has a bad-day path and a 30-minute unit cap: it is applying the lesson it teaches to itself.
Fluctuating capacity recurs unpredictably and doesn't resolve. The fix is almost always the same shape: let state survive an interruption nobody can schedule around.

title: Cognitive and Energy-Limited Access, Routinely Forgotten
description: The access needs with no assistive technology to point at — memory load, unclear structure, and the energy an interface costs — and why 'the user was just tired' is often a design finding wearing a dismissal.

learningObjectives.text: Name specific cognitive access needs a design has to account for
Diagnose why a form with no clear defect produces high abandonment
Argue that energy cost is a legitimate access dimension, not a mood

contentSections.title: The access need with no button to press

contentSections.body: There's no screen reader for cognitive load. No zoom level fixes a form that asks you to remember what you entered on page one while filling in page four. This access need is real, and there's no assistive technology stall to point at for it — the design either respects it or it doesn't, with nothing between the person and the barrier.

Cognitive access needs include: memory load (holding information across steps), unclear or unpredictable structure, jargon and unexplained terms, time pressure, attention and executive function differences (including ADHD), dyslexia, intellectual disability, and — squarely inside this population — brain fog from chronic illness, chronic pain, or medication side effects.

WCAG covers a real but thin slice of this directly (2.2's timing criteria, 3.1's readability guidance), which is exactly why a clean WCAG conformance report can sit next to a form nobody with brain fog can get through. Phase 3 of this track goes deep on cognitive and content accessibility specifically; this lesson's job is narrower — making sure it's on your map at all, this early, as its own category rather than a footnote to motor or sensory access.

contentSections.question: Which WCAG 2.2 success criterion requires a multi-step process to show a progress indicator?
contentSections.hint: Check 2.2's timing criteria and 3.2's predictability criteria before you answer — think about what they actually require versus what would be nice to have.
contentSections.answer: None does. WCAG has criteria for giving users control over *timing* (2.2.1, 2.2.6) and for predictable navigation (3.2.3), but no success criterion requires a progress indicator, a step counter, or feedback on how much of a task remains. A multi-page form with zero sense of progress can conform fully to WCAG 2.2 AA. This is exactly the gap that makes cognitive-load findings the ones a scan will never surface.

contentSections.scenario: A four-page government form has no progress indicator, and validation errors appear only after the final submit — a user who mistyped their date of birth on page one only finds out on page four, after re-entering everything else. There is no missing alt text, no keyboard trap, no contrast failure. Every WCAG automated check passes.
contentSections.question: The form has a high abandonment rate. What's the mechanism?

options.label: Users are giving up out of impatience, unrelated to accessibility
The form exceeds the memory and re-orientation capacity a meaningful share of users have available, independent of any assistive technology
The scan is misconfigured and missing real defects

feedback.cogload: Right. Nothing here trips a WCAG success criterion cleanly, and nothing here requires assistive technology to fail against it. The barrier is structural: no sense of progress, no early warning of errors, and a design that assumes the user can hold four pages of context in working memory with nothing lost along the way. Someone with ADHD, someone with chronic-illness brain fog, someone simply unfamiliar with government forms — all fail this the same way, for the same design reason.
feedback.impatience: "Impatience" quietly relocates the failure back into the user, the exact move the previous lesson was about catching. The form is asking for a specific cognitive resource — sustained working memory across four unconnected pages with no feedback — that isn't evenly distributed, and running out of it isn't impatience.
feedback.misconfigured: The scan is probably working correctly. That's the point of this lesson: this class of barrier passes automated and even most manual conformance checks cleanly, because nothing in WCAG's testable criteria captures "can a person hold this much in their head."

contentSections.mechanism: **Cognitive load is invisible to conformance checking and real anyway.** A progress indicator, inline validation, and clear, plain-language error messages don't map to a single clean success criterion the way missing alt text does — which means this whole category is systematically under-represented in audits that are organised around citable criteria, exactly the gap the previous module's lesson on "findings without a clean criterion" was built to catch.

contentSections.body: Cognitive load barriers pass most conformance checks cleanly and are real anyway. Write them as findings even when no criterion names them.

contentSections.title: Energy as an access need, not a mood

contentSections.body: A product manager says, dismissing a finding: "That's not an accessibility issue — the user was just tired." The user has POTS. Being tired, for her, is not a mood. It's her baseline, and the interface either fits inside it or she doesn't finish the task.

contentSections.scenario: A product's core flow has several patterns already in place. Judge each one on whether it costs a meaningful share of a limited energy budget.
contentSections.question: Select every pattern below that imposes a real energy cost worth naming in a finding.

items.label: A dashboard that auto-refreshes every 30 seconds, resetting scroll position and any open dropdown
A single unsegmented 40-field form with no save point anywhere in it
An application that must be completed in one sitting, with no resume mechanism
A settings page that autosaves every field individually as it's edited
An error state that tells the user exactly what to fix and lets them fix just that field
A checkout that discards the whole cart and asks the user to rebuild it after a payment failure

explanation.autorefresh: Costs real energy: every 30 seconds, whatever the user was doing — reading, scrolling, mid-thought — gets interrupted and has to be re-found. For someone managing a fixed daily budget of attention, an interruption every half-minute is a design choice with a real bill attached.
explanation.onelongform: Forces the user to hold the whole task's context for as long as it takes to finish, with no honest stopping point. This is the direct energy-cost analogue of the fluctuating-capacity problem from the previous lesson.
explanation.onesitting: Same shape again: it assumes a continuous block of capacity exists, which is precisely the assumption a fluctuating or fatigue-limited user cannot rely on.
explanation.saveresume: This is the pattern that *reduces* cost — cited here as the counter-example. Autosave-per-field means no re-entry, no lost work, no penalty for stopping.
explanation.clearrecovery: Also cost-reducing: a precise, scoped error state means fixing one thing instead of redoing several, which is the difference between a five-second correction and a five-minute one.
explanation.revalidate: A meaningful, avoidable cost: it turns one failed payment attempt into a second full task (rebuilding a cart) on top of the first. The two failure-recovery items above show what this should look like instead.

contentSections.synthesis: Four of the six cost something real; two actively reduce cost. The pattern behind the four: each one either forces re-work after an interruption or assumes continuous capacity nobody actually has continuously. Naming this as "energy cost" rather than "minor UX friction" is what phase 3's module on this exact topic is going to teach you to defend as a real finding, not a nice-to-have.

contentSections.body: This lesson isn't asking you to count interactions yet — that's a full module later in the track ("The Energy Cost of an Interface," phase 3). What it's asking for now is smaller and foundational: treat energy as a legitimate access axis, on the same list as vision, hearing and motor, rather than as a soft complaint that gets cut from a report when space runs short. A user who has to lie down mid-task is not describing a mood. They're describing what this interface costs them to operate — which is a design fact, exactly like contrast ratio is.

contentSections.question: A product manager reviewing your finding about the 30-second auto-refresh says: "This isn't an accessibility bug, it's just annoying." What's the one-sentence reply that keeps this a design finding rather than a complaint?
contentSections.hint: What does the interruption cost, specifically, for someone with a fixed daily budget of attention or energy — and is that cost evenly distributed across users?
contentSections.answer: "For most users it's annoying; for someone budgeting a fixed amount of attention or energy per day, an interruption every thirty seconds is a real, measurable cost that can be the difference between finishing the task and not — which is exactly what an accessibility finding is for." The reply doesn't argue the annoyance away. It names who the annoyance becomes a barrier for, and why.

contentSections.body: Energy is an access axis with real design consequences — interruptions, forced re-entry, no honest stopping point — not a soft complaint to leave out of the report.

title: Where Designers Acquire the Assumptions That Cause Barriers
description: Tracing a shipped barrier back to the specific point in a design process where an assumption about the user got baked in — and where it's cheapest to catch.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a specific barrier back to the assumption that produced it
Recognise the default persona as a design fiction that silently excludes access needs
Identify the cheapest point in a process to interrupt a barrier-producing assumption

contentSections.body: A design system sets minimum body text at 14px because "that's what looks clean on the mockup." Nobody in the room has low vision. Nobody asks who that number excludes. Six months and forty screens later, changing it means touching all forty.

contentSections.scenario: A project kickoff deck includes a persona: "Alex, 28, tech-savvy, always on the latest phone." Every subsequent design decision — font size, interaction pattern, expected task speed — gets justified by reference to what "Alex" would find intuitive.
contentSections.question: What's the risk in using this persona as the design's reference point?

options.label: Personas are inherently bad design tools and should be dropped
Alex silently encodes an assumption of full vision, hearing, mobility and cognition, unless the persona says otherwise
There's no risk — personas are just a communication device, not a spec

feedback.silent: Yes. "Tech-savvy" and "28" say nothing about vision, hearing, motor ability or cognitive load — and because nothing is said, the team's mental model fills in the unstated default, which in practice is almost always full-capacity, non-disabled, sighted, hearing, unimpaired attention. Every decision justified by "what Alex would expect" then quietly inherits that default, without anyone deciding to exclude anyone.
feedback.dropall: Personas aren't the problem; an unexamined default is. A persona that explicitly includes a range of access needs — or several personas that do — is a genuinely useful tool for keeping a team's mental model honest.
feedback.norisk: It functions as a spec whether or not anyone intends it to: "what would Alex do" becomes the sentence that settles font size, timeout length and interaction pattern in meeting after meeting. An unstated assumption used that often is doing real design work.

contentSections.concept: **The default persona problem**: any persona (or any absence of one, which just defaults to "me, the designer") that doesn't explicitly name a range of access needs will, by omission, encode the designer's own capacities as universal. This isn't usually a decision anyone makes on purpose — it's what happens when nobody in the room has to ask the question, because nobody in the room needs the answer for themselves.

contentSections.body:
The assumption gets baked in at several specific, nameable points — worth knowing because each one is a different, specific place to intervene:

- **Research recruitment.** Who gets invited to user interviews? A recruitment brief that doesn't specify disabled participants will, statistically, mostly not get them.
- **Personas.** As above — silence defaults to non-disabled.
- **Design system defaults.** Contrast ratios, font sizes, spacing set once and inherited everywhere. Get these numbers right early and dozens of screens are correct by default; get them wrong and every screen inherits the defect.
- **Review process.** If nobody in a design review has lived experience of a disability, or the authority to block a ship on accessibility grounds, the review checks for things the room already knows to look for — usually excluding this category entirely.
- **Timeline pressure.** When scope shrinks near a deadline, accessibility work is disproportionately the first thing cut, because it was never on the critical path to a demo looking finished.
The default is never neutral. Silence about access needs in research, personas and design defaults fills in with "me, the designer" every time.
The cheapest place to catch a barrier is before a single pixel is drawn. The most expensive is in production, after forty screens have inherited the same broken default.

contentSections.question: A design-system contrast token gets fixed the day it's flagged, before dev starts. A different team catches the same defect three sprints after launch. Roughly how much more work does the second team face?
contentSections.hint: Think about how many screens inherit a shared token by the time a defect is caught post-launch versus pre-build.
contentSections.answer: Not "a bit more" — an order of magnitude more, typically. The pre-build fix is one number in one file. The post-launch fix is that same number, plus finding and re-testing every screen that already shipped with the wrong one, plus whatever downstream content was laid out assuming the broken value. The fix itself didn't get harder. The number of places it has to be verified did.

contentSections.title: The design review that's already "basically done"
contentSections.opening: You're the accessibility reviewer brought into a design review two days before a build starts. The design is polished, the stakeholders are pleased, and you notice the body text is 12px at a contrast ratio of 3.4:1 against the background — well under the 4.5:1 WCAG AA requires for normal text. Nobody in the room has raised it.

raise.situation: You raise it. The lead designer, visibly tired after a long sprint, says: "We're two days from dev start. Can we just fix the contrast in a follow-up ticket after launch?"
raise.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Agree — a follow-up ticket, don't block the timeline
choices.consequence: The build starts on schedule. The follow-up ticket is triaged three sprints later, after the same 12px/3.4:1 pairing has been implemented across every screen in the design system that inherited this one.

choices.label: Insist the whole design go back to research before dev starts
choices.consequence: This is a much bigger ask than the actual problem — one number, in one place, in the design system's type scale — and it reads as disproportionate. The team pushes back hard and the relationship with this designer gets harder for the rest of the project.

choices.label: Name the exact fix, the exact place it lives, and the cost of not making it now
choices.consequence: You point out this is one token in the type scale — one number, one place — not a redesign, and that it's inherited by every screen the moment dev starts building from it. A ten-minute change now versus a multi-screen retrofit later.

response.situation: The designer checks: it is, in fact, a single design-token value. She updates it before the meeting ends.
response.question: What's the lesson worth carrying forward?

choices.label: Note it and move to the next review
choices.consequence: The fix ships correct from day one, at the cost of a ten-minute conversation instead of a multi-screen retrofit.

deferred.summary: The follow-up ticket becomes a multi-screen retrofit, because the design-system token was already load-bearing everywhere by the time anyone got to it.
deferred.lesson: "Fix it later" on a design-system-level default is rarely later — it's the same fix, at a much higher cost, applied retroactively to every place that already inherited it. The two-day timeline pressure that made deferring tempting was the exact reason to fix it now, not the reason to wait.

overcorrected.summary: The actual defect — one number — gets lost inside a much larger, harder-to-agree-on ask, and trust with this designer takes real damage for a fix that should have taken ten minutes.
overcorrected.lesson: Scale the intervention to the actual size of the problem. A one-token fix and a full redesign are different asks with different costs, and treating the first as if it were the second burns credibility you'll want on the next, genuinely harder finding.

resolved.summary: One number, changed once, before it propagated. No retrofit, no lost goodwill.
resolved.lesson: The intervention that works names three things: the exact defect, the exact place it lives, and what it costs to fix now versus later. That's usually a shorter conversation than either deferring or escalating, and it's the version that gets the fix made in the room.

contentSections.body: A design-system default is cheap to fix before it propagates and expensive after. Name the exact defect, the exact place it lives, and the cost of waiting — that's usually the whole conversation.

title: Practice — Barriers, Access Needs and Assumptions
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where naming the design fact instead of the deficit stops being something you have to think about.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite deficit-framed observations as barrier-framed findings at speed
Classify access needs by category and by the design fix each one calls for

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing is timed and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Map the Access Needs One Real Product Must Serve
description: Produce a needs map for a real product: every access category it has to serve, and one concrete, specific failure example per need — the document that turns 'we should be accessible' into a scoped list of what to check.

learningObjectives.text: Inventory the full range of access needs a specific product must serve
Produce a concrete failure example per access need, not a generic description

contentSections.body: "We should think about accessibility" is a sentence that produces nothing. "Here are the eleven access needs this product has to serve, and here's what currently fails each one" is a sentence a team can act on this sprint. This lab produces the second sentence.

contentSections.title: Your needs map
contentSections.brief: Pick one real product you can actually examine — something you use, something you're building, or a public site you can explore freely. You are producing the document a team would want *before* a design review starts: not a list of WCAG criteria, but a list of the actual access needs this specific product has to serve, each one paired with a real, current or plausible failure.
contentSections.deliverable: A needs map: every relevant access category for this product, one concrete failure example per category, drawn from the four-way framework (permanent / temporary / situational / fluctuating) and the cognitive/energy categories from this module.

stages.title: Choose the product and list its core tasks
stages.instructions: Name the product and the two or three tasks that matter most in it (not every feature — the two or three things it exists to let someone do). Everything in the rest of this lab attaches to these tasks, not to the product in the abstract.
stages.checkpoint: You have a named product and 2-3 named core tasks written down.

stages.title: Inventory the access needs relevant to those tasks
stages.instructions: Working from this module's categories — vision, hearing, motor, cognitive, speech, and fluctuating/energy — list every one that's genuinely relevant to completing the core tasks you named. For each, note whether the specific instance you're thinking of is permanent, temporary, situational or fluctuating (some categories will have more than one).
stages.checkpoint: Every entry names a category and where it sits on the permanent/temporary/situational/fluctuating axis.

stages.title: Find or predict one concrete failure per need
stages.instructions: For each access need on your list, either test the product yourself against it (keyboard-only, screen reader, 400% zoom, whatever fits) or, where you can't test directly, specify precisely what a failure would look like and why you expect it — grounded in something about this specific product's actual implementation, not a generic statement. "Might be a problem" is not a failure example; "the date picker has no keyboard alternative to dragging" is.
stages.checkpoint: Every access need has one specific, checkable failure example attached — real if you tested it, precisely predicted if you didn't.

stages.title: Write the needs map
stages.instructions: Assemble it as a short table or list: access need, category (permanent/temporary/situational/fluctuating), the concrete failure example, and one line on what a minimal fix would look like. This is the document, not a draft of one — write it as something you'd actually hand to a team.
stages.checkpoint: The document is complete, specific throughout, and contains no need without a matching concrete example.

rubric.criterion: Every major access category is represented
rubric.meets: Vision, hearing, motor, cognitive, and fluctuating/energy all appear, unless a specific one is genuinely irrelevant to this product's core tasks — and that omission is stated, not silent.

rubric.criterion: Every need has a concrete failure example
rubric.meets: No entry says only "could be an issue" — each names a specific interaction, element or state, tested or precisely predicted.

rubric.criterion: The permanent/temporary/situational/fluctuating axis is used, not just named
rubric.meets: At least one entry per axis category where it genuinely applies to this product's real users.

rubric.criterion: Language locates the barrier in the design, not the person
rubric.meets: Every failure example is written the way lesson one taught — a design fact, not a deficit statement about a user.

rubric.criterion: It's usable, not academic
rubric.meets: A team could open this document and know exactly what to check and where, without you in the room to explain it.

contentSections.body: A needs map turns "we should think about accessibility" into a checkable list. That's the whole value of the document — specificity, not comprehensiveness for its own sake.

title: Checkpoint — How Barriers Get Built
description: Ten questions pulling across this module and the previous one. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and the previous module's finding procedure without looking them up

questions.from: This module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: What is a barrier, in the vocabulary this module uses?

options.label: A fact about a body or mind
A fact about a design that stops an impairment and an environment from getting along
A synonym for disability

questions.explanation: Impairment is the fact about the body. Barrier is the fact about the design. Disability is what happens when the two meet — and it's the barrier, not the impairment, that's yours to fix.

questions.from: This module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: A finding says "blind users are limited on this page." What's the fix to the finding itself, before any code changes?

options.label: Nothing — the observation is accurate as written
Relocate the problem from the user to the specific missing design element
Add a WCAG citation and leave the wording otherwise unchanged

questions.explanation: "Blind users are limited" names a deficit in the user with no design fact attached. The rewrite names what's actually missing — an alt attribute, a role, a label — which is the thing a developer can act on.

questions.from: This module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: Which of these is a situational, not permanent, access need?

options.label: Congenital blindness
Reading a phone screen in direct sunlight
A relapsing chronic illness with unpredictable bad days

questions.explanation: Situational needs come from the environment, not the body, and resolve the moment the environment changes — go indoors and the glare is gone. Congenital blindness is permanent; a relapsing illness is fluctuating.

questions.from: This module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a fluctuating access need from a temporary one?

options.label: Fluctuating needs are more severe
A temporary need resolves and stays resolved; a fluctuating one recurs unpredictably, indefinitely
There's no real difference — both are short-term
