questions.explanation: A cast comes off and stays off. A fluctuating condition's bad day comes back on no fixed schedule, which is why the design fix (state survives interruption, no punishing timeouts) has to hold indefinitely, not just during a known recovery window.

questions.from: This module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: A multi-page form has no accessibility-scan-detectable defects and still produces high abandonment. What's the most likely mechanism?

options.label: Users are simply impatient
Cognitive load — memory demand and lack of feedback — exceeds what a meaningful share of users can hold, independent of assistive technology
The scan must be misconfigured

questions.explanation: Cognitive load barriers routinely pass conformance checks cleanly, because most testable WCAG criteria don't capture memory demand or structural unpredictability. That doesn't make the barrier less real.

questions.from: Previous module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: In the finding procedure from the previous module, what comes first?

options.label: The success criterion
The task the user was trying to complete
The severity rating

questions.explanation: Task, access method, where it stops, what they're left with, citation — in that order. Starting from the criterion produces technically complete audits nobody can prioritise.

questions.from: Previous module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Roughly what share of accessibility barriers does an automated scanner detect on a typical site?

options.label: About 30%, and the figure depends heavily on how you count
About 90%
Essentially all of them if the tool is configured well

questions.explanation: Somewhere in the 20-40% range. Scanners are near-complete on markup properties and structurally blind to meaning, layout and runtime behaviour.

questions.from: Previous module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Why does fluency with an assistive technology sometimes make a reviewer miss barriers, not just find more of them?

options.label: Fluent reviewers stop caring about accessibility over time
Expertise is a workaround — a barrier you've learned to route around can stop registering as a barrier
It doesn't; fluency only ever improves what a reviewer finds

questions.explanation: The barriers a fluent reviewer stops noticing are systematically the ones that hit people newer to the technology than they are — a large, normal population, not an edge case.

questions.from: Previous module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Which reader of an audit needs the scope statement — including what wasn't tested — the most?

options.label: The developer fixing an individual ticket
A procurement reviewer comparing suppliers, who may never read a single finding
Nobody — scope statements are a formality

questions.explanation: Accessibility statements are self-declared, so a procurement reviewer's whole basis for trusting one is the evidence behind it. An audit's scope section can end up doing more real-world work than its findings.

questions.from: Previous module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: What belongs in a message to a client when you can't deliver the scope you agreed?

options.label: A description of the health event that caused it
The gap, costed options, a recommendation, and a decision deadline
A brief apology and a promise to catch up

questions.explanation: The client needs a decision, and a diagnosis isn't a variable they can act on. State the gap, price the options, recommend one, set a deadline.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Principles, Guidelines, Criteria, Techniques: What Each Is For
description: WCAG's four layers do four different jobs, only one of which is testable and citable — and techniques, the layer most people quote as if it were the rule, aren't the rule at all.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish WCAG's four layers and what each is for
Identify which layer is the testable, citable unit in a finding
Explain why meeting an unlisted technique can still satisfy a success criterion

contentSections.body: A finding reads: "This page fails WCAG." Fails which part? WCAG is not one rule — it's four layers stacked on top of each other, and only one of those layers is something a page can actually pass or fail.

contentSections.scenario: A product image on an e-commerce page has no `alt` attribute at all. You need to write this up as a finding with a citation.
contentSections.question: Which layer of WCAG do you cite?

options.label: Principle 1: Perceivable
Guideline 1.1: Text Alternatives
Success Criterion 1.1.1: Non-text Content

feedback.criterion: Right. Success criteria are the only layer written as a testable pass/fail statement — 1.1.1 requires that non-text content have a text alternative, with a small set of named exceptions. "This image has no alt attribute" is a direct, checkable failure of that specific sentence.
feedback.principle: Perceivable is one of four organising ideas (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) that group guidelines together. It's real and useful for structuring a report's table of contents. It is not testable — nothing about "Perceivable" alone tells you what passes or fails.
feedback.guideline: Closer, but still one level too abstract. Guideline 1.1, "Text Alternatives," states a goal ("provide text alternatives for non-text content") without the specific, testable conditions that make a check possible. The success criterion underneath it is what supplies those conditions.

contentSections.concept:
WCAG has four layers, and each does a different job:

**Principles** (4 total: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust — "POUR") — the top-level organising idea. Not testable.

**Guidelines** (13, grouped under the principles) — a broad goal, like "1.1 Text Alternatives" or "2.4 Navigable." States intent, still not testable on its own.

**Success criteria** — the testable layer, numbered like `1.1.1`, `2.4.7`, `4.1.2`. Each is a specific, checkable statement with a conformance level (A, AA or AAA). This is what you cite in a finding.

**Techniques** — informative, non-normative documentation of specific ways to meet a criterion (or specific ways it fails). Covered fully in the pod after this one.

contentSections.code:
Finding #7
Severity: High
This page fails WCAG Principle 1: Perceivable.
Recommendation: review content for perceivability issues.
contentSections.question: What's wrong with how this finding is written?

options.label: It cites a principle instead of a testable success criterion
The severity should be Medium, not High
It should also cite a technique document

feedback.toohigh: Correct. "Fails Principle 1: Perceivable" isn't a testable claim — a principle groups thirteen guidelines and dozens of success criteria under one word. A developer reading this has no idea what to check, let alone what to fix. The finding needs to drop down two layers to a specific success criterion: which element, which SC, why it fails that SC's specific text.
feedback.severity: Severity is impossible to assess sensibly here, for the same underlying reason: you can't rate the severity of a defect you haven't located yet. Fix the citation first.
feedback.technique: A technique reference would help once the finding names an actual success criterion — but citing a technique on top of a principle doesn't fix the core problem, which is that no testable unit has been identified at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the citation-layer version of the previous module's "where" problem: a finding that cites the wrong layer of abstraction is exactly as unusable as one that names no location at all. "Perceivable" is true of roughly a third of WCAG's entire success criteria — it identifies nothing a developer can act on.

contentSections.body: Principles and guidelines organise the standard. Success criteria are what you test against and cite. Get comfortable naming the criterion, not the chapter it lives in.

A developer says: "We used technique G18 for contrast, so we comply." Using a technique is one way to meet a criterion. It is not the same statement as meeting the criterion — and the gap between those two claims is where a lot of false confidence lives.

contentSections.scenario: A team builds a custom date picker using a technique not documented anywhere in WCAG's technique library — a genuinely novel keyboard interaction pattern they invented. It works: every function is fully keyboard-operable, focus moves sensibly, and screen readers announce state changes correctly. An auditor flags it: "This isn't a listed sufficient technique, so it fails 2.1.1 Keyboard."
contentSections.question: Is the auditor right?

options.label: Yes — only listed techniques count as meeting a success criterion
No — success criteria are normative; techniques are informative examples, not an exhaustive list of what's allowed
It depends on whether the technique is later added to the WCAG techniques document

feedback.nolisted: Correct, and this is the single most common misunderstanding about how WCAG actually works. The success criterion — 2.1.1, "all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface" — is the normative requirement. Techniques are the W3C's documented, non-exhaustive examples of ways to meet it. A genuinely novel approach that satisfies the criterion's actual text satisfies the criterion, whether or not the W3C has written a technique document about it yet.
feedback.yeslisted: This reverses the actual relationship between the two documents. If it were true, no new interaction pattern could ever conform to WCAG until the W3C caught up and wrote a technique for it — which would make the standard unable to keep pace with real interface design, and that's not how it's built.
feedback.depends: Conformance doesn't wait on documentation. The criterion is met or not met based on its own text, evaluated against the actual behaviour of the control, the moment it ships — not based on whether a technique document exists yet.

contentSections.mechanism: **Only the success criteria themselves are normative** — the actual pass/fail requirement. Everything else in WCAG's supporting material (Techniques, Understanding WCAG, the technique-specific Failures documents) is informative: helpful, W3C-vetted, and not an exhaustive or mandatory list. A **sufficient technique** is one documented way to pass; a **failure** is a documented way to fail; neither list claims completeness. The practical upshot for a reviewer: when you can't find a listed technique for what you're looking at, the question is still "does this meet the criterion's actual text," not "is this on the list."

contentSections.body: Success criteria are the requirement. Techniques are documented examples of how to meet or fail it — helpful, and not the whole universe of what's allowed.

title: Levels A, AA and AAA and What Conformance Claims Mean
description: Why AA is the working baseline almost everywhere, why AAA isn't simply 'more accessible,' and what a conformance claim actually asserts once you read it literally.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what distinguishes Level A, AA and AAA criteria
State why AAA conformance is not recommended as a site-wide target
Identify what a WCAG conformance claim does and doesn't assert

contentSections.body: A client asks: "Why are we only targeting AA? Isn't more accessible always better — why not go for AAA?" It's a reasonable question with a specific, non-obvious answer.

WCAG's three levels are not simply "mild, moderate, severe" — they're a rough ordering of how broadly achievable a criterion is across every kind of content:

- **Level A** — the baseline. Criteria the W3C considers achievable for essentially all content, with real, significant user impact if unmet (e.g. 1.1.1 Non-text Content, 2.1.1 Keyboard).
- **Level AA** — the standard most legal frameworks reference (EN 301 549, most interpretations of the ADA, Section 508). Broadly achievable, and this is where most real accessibility work lives (e.g. 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum, 2.4.7 Focus Visible).
- **Level AAA** — the highest bar, and WCAG's own conformance section explicitly states it is **not recommended as a general policy for entire sites**, because some AAA criteria genuinely cannot be satisfied for certain kinds of content (sign-language interpretation for all audio, for instance) without changing what the content fundamentally is.

A severity mistake worth naming directly: a Level A criterion is not automatically "worse" to fail than a Level AA one. Level correlates loosely with how universally achievable a criterion is, not with how much a given failure hurts a given user. A Level AA contrast failure on the only button in a checkout flow can be a harder blocker than a Level A failure on a decorative element nobody needs.

contentSections.scenario: You're explaining WCAG's structure to a new team member who assumes the three levels split roughly evenly.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of WCAG 2.2's success criteria are Level A (the baseline tier)?
contentSections.explanation: It's close to a third, with AA and AAA splitting the rest — AAA actually carries the largest single share, precisely because it includes many criteria the W3C judged too demanding or context-dependent to require universally. The number worth remembering isn't the exact split; it's that the levels track achievability across all content types, not a severity ranking you can read straight off the letter grade.

contentSections.body: AA is the working legal and practical baseline almost everywhere. AAA site-wide is explicitly discouraged by WCAG itself — and level is not the same axis as severity.

contentSections.title: What a conformance claim actually asserts

contentSections.body: "Our site conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA." Read that sentence the way a lawyer would, not the way a marketing page does — it's making a much narrower claim than it sounds like.

contentSections.scenario: A company states: "Our checkout flow conforms to WCAG 2.1 Level AA." Judge each statement about what that claim does or doesn't actually assert.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that correctly describes what this conformance claim asserts.

items.label: Every Level A and Level AA success criterion is met across the defined scope (the checkout flow)
The entire website, not just checkout, is covered by the claim
Third-party content embedded in checkout (e.g. an iframe'd payment widget) they don't control is automatically included
Every real user, on every combination of browser and assistive technology, will find the flow fully usable
The claim describes the state of the flow at a specific point in time — later changes could invalidate it silently
It says nothing about Level AAA criteria one way or the other

explanation.allcriteria: This is the actual content of the claim: every applicable Level A and AA criterion, met, within the stated scope. Nothing less counts as conformance — WCAG conformance is all-or-nothing per criterion within scope, not a percentage.
explanation.everypage: The claim is scoped explicitly to "the checkout flow." A conformance claim only covers what it says it covers — this is exactly why the previous module's lesson on scope statements matters so much at procurement.
explanation.thirdparty: WCAG's own conformance requirements exclude content the organisation doesn't have the authority to change, unless they've taken on that responsibility explicitly. An embedded third-party widget usually needs its own separate claim.
explanation.usable: Conformance to testable criteria is not the same claim as "everyone can use this" — this is the whole distinction the first module of this track was built around: passing testable criteria and being usable are related, overlapping, and not identical.
explanation.pointintime: Correct and easy to forget: a conformance claim describes a snapshot. The next deploy that changes the checkout flow can silently break it, and nothing about the original claim updates itself.
explanation.aaa: Right — an AA claim makes no assertion about AAA criteria at all, in either direction. It's neither claiming nor disclaiming them.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six describe what the claim actually says; three describe what people commonly assume it says. The gap between those two lists is exactly why an audit's scope section — what was tested, on what, at what point in time — carries as much weight as its findings.

contentSections.body: A conformance claim asserts every criterion at that level was met, within the stated scope, at a point in time — and nothing beyond that scope, however the sentence reads.

title: Reading a Success Criterion Literally
description: Success criteria are written with exceptions, thresholds and qualifiers that carry real weight — reading past them is how a criterion gets misapplied in both directions.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a success criterion's exact wording, including its exceptions, to a specific case
Identify when an exception clause actually applies versus when it's being used to excuse a real failure

contentSections.title: The words mean exactly what they say

contentSections.body: "Contrast has to be 4.5:1." Said like that, it sounds like a universal number. The actual text of SC 1.4.3 has three carve-outs in it — large text, incidental text, and logotypes — and skipping past them produces both false positives and false negatives in a report.

contentSections.problem: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), read literally: "The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for: Large Text (at least 3:1); Incidental (text that is part of an inactive UI component, pure decoration, not visible to anyone, or part of an image with other significant visual content, no requirement); Logotypes (text in a logo, no requirement)." You're reviewing a pricing page where the plan name ("Pro") renders at 28px bold, contrast ratio 3.2:1.

steps.label: Identify which clause applies
steps.work: 28px bold qualifies as "large text" under WCAG's definition (at least 18pt, or 14pt bold — 28px ≈ 21pt, comfortably over the threshold), so the 3:1 ratio applies, not 4.5:1.
steps.why: Reading past the size qualifier is the single most common contrast-check error — treating every piece of text with the same 4.5:1 bar regardless of size.

steps.label: Check the measured value against the correct threshold
steps.work: 3.2:1 measured against a 3:1 requirement for large text.
steps.why: This is the step that actually resolves the finding — and it resolves it as a pass, which a reviewer using the wrong threshold would have missed.

steps.label: State the verdict precisely
steps.work: Passes SC 1.4.3 — 3.2:1 exceeds the 3:1 minimum for large text. Would fail if the same 3.2:1 ratio applied to body copy at 16px regular weight.
steps.why: Writing the verdict with the applicable threshold named protects the finding from being second-guessed by someone who checks it against the wrong number later.

faded.problem: Same page, second case: a copyright line in the footer reads "© 2026 Northwind Retail" at 12px regular weight, contrast ratio 3.8:1.

blanks.prompt: Which clause of SC 1.4.3 applies here — large text, incidental, logotype, or the default 4.5:1?
blanks.why: 12px regular is well under the large-text threshold (18pt/14pt bold), it's genuine body copy rather than decoration, and it isn't a logo — so none of the three exceptions apply.

blanks.prompt: Does 3.8:1 pass or fail against that threshold?
blanks.why: 3.8:1 is below the 4.5:1 required for normal text — a real, citable failure, not a borderline case.

blanks.prompt: In one sentence, what would make a reviewer wrongly pass this?
blanks.answer: assuming footer text counts as incidental or decorative without checking the actual definition
accept: treating footer copy as decorative by assumption
blanks.why: "It's just a footer" is not one of WCAG's three exceptions. The incidental exception is narrow — inactive UI, pure decoration, or content already covered by significant surrounding imagery — and a footer copyright line meets none of those conditions.

contentSections.procedure: **Identify which clause of the criterion's actual text applies → check the measured value against the correct threshold → state the verdict against the specific clause you used.** Skipping the first step is how both errors happen: applying 4.5:1 to text that qualifies for the 3:1 large-text exception produces a false failure, and assuming an exception applies without checking its actual conditions produces a false pass.

contentSections.body: A success criterion's exceptions are part of the criterion, not an escape hatch to argue about later. Check which clause actually applies before you measure anything.

Someone assumes every decorative image can just skip alt text, full stop. That's close to SC 1.1.1's actual carve-out — but not quite it, and the gap between "close to" and "actually it" is where a real finding hides.

contentSections.scenario: A product page has a large hero photograph of the product in use — someone wearing the jacket being sold, on a mountain trail, in dramatic light. The developer marks it `alt=""` (empty alt, the pattern for pure decoration), reasoning: "it's just a mood photo, the product info is in the text below."
contentSections.question: Is empty alt the correct choice here?

options.label: Yes — SC 1.1.1's decorative-image exception clearly applies
No — this image conveys meaningful information (context, styling, use case) that empty alt discards entirely
It doesn't matter — hero images are rarely checked in practice

feedback.noempty: Right. SC 1.1.1's exception is for content that is "pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users" — a divider line, a background texture. A hero photo showing the actual product in a real context is conveying information a sighted user gets and a screen reader user, with empty alt, does not: what it looks like worn, the setting it's marketed for, the mood the brand is selling. That's not decoration; it's content, and it needs a real (if concise) description.
feedback.yesempty: This is the exception being applied to something it wasn't written for. "It's just a mood photo" describes the image's *purpose* in the page's marketing, not whether it conveys information — and it plainly does, which is the actual test 1.1.1 sets.
feedback.irrelevant: Frequency of manual checking has no bearing on whether the criterion applies. This is also exactly the kind of judgement call — does this convey meaning or not — that an automated scan can never make, since it requires understanding what the image shows.

contentSections.concept: **An exception clause has its own conditions, and meeting the general shape of the exception ("it's decorative-ish") isn't the same as meeting its actual definition.** The 1.1.1 decorative exception is narrow on purpose: purely visual formatting, or genuinely not conveying information beyond what's already in surrounding text. A photo doing real communicative work — showing context, evoking use, standing in for description — needs a text alternative, even when a marketer would call it "just an image."

contentSections.body: An exception applies when its actual, narrow conditions are met — not whenever something merely resembles the category the exception describes.

title: Understanding Documents and Techniques: Advisory, Not Law
description: What each of WCAG's three supporting document types actually is — normative requirement, non-normative explanation, and non-normative example — and why the difference changes what you can insist on.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the normative WCAG text from its non-normative supporting documents
Resolve a dispute about whether an unlisted approach satisfies a criterion

contentSections.body: A developer opens three tabs — the WCAG spec, an "Understanding" page, and a Techniques page — and asks which one is actually the rule. Only one of the three is.

WCAG's ecosystem has three layers of document, and they carry different weight:

- **The WCAG success criteria themselves** (the normative text) — the actual requirement. This is what a conformance claim is measured against.
- **Understanding WCAG** — a non-normative companion document per criterion, explaining intent, rationale, who it helps, and how to think about edge cases. Genuinely useful for interpretation disputes; not itself a testable rule.
- **Techniques for WCAG** — non-normative, specific implementation patterns, split into **sufficient techniques** (documented ways to meet a criterion), **advisory techniques** (recommended best practice beyond the minimum), and **failures** (documented patterns that fail a criterion, cited as an `F` number like F65 or F77).

The hierarchy that matters in a dispute: cite the success criterion's own text first. Use Understanding WCAG to argue intent when the wording is ambiguous. Use Techniques to illustrate — never to argue that something not on the list is automatically non-compliant, which is the mistake the previous lesson's diagnose-mechanism exercise walked through directly.

contentSections.scenario: An accessibility consultant tells a team: "Your carousel doesn't use technique SCR33, so it fails 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide." The team's carousel does, in fact, let users pause auto-advancing content — just through a different script pattern than SCR33 documents.
contentSections.question: Is the consultant's reasoning sound?

options.label: Yes — SCR33 is the documented technique for this criterion, so an alternative approach doesn't count
No — the criterion's actual requirement (a mechanism to pause, stop or hide) is what matters, and the team's carousel provides one
It depends on whether SCR33 is marked "sufficient" or "advisory"

feedback.nosound: Correct — and this is the same structural mistake as citing an unlisted technique as automatic failure for keyboard operability. SC 2.2.2 requires that moving, blinking, scrolling or auto-updating content have a mechanism for the user to pause, stop or hide it. If the team's script genuinely provides that mechanism and it works, the criterion is met, full stop, regardless of which named technique (if any) their implementation resembles.
feedback.yessound: This treats a technique document as if it were the requirement rather than one example of meeting the requirement — exactly the confusion this module exists to clear up.
feedback.depends: SCR33 is listed as a sufficient technique either way; the distinction between sufficient and advisory doesn't change the underlying point, which is that sufficient techniques are examples, not an exhaustive gate.

contentSections.mechanism: This is the same normative/informative split as the previous lesson, applied to a dispute rather than a definition: **the criterion's text is what a page is measured against.** A technique document is evidence that a particular approach works — never proof that an approach not on the list doesn't.

contentSections.body: Success criteria are normative. Understanding WCAG and the Techniques documents are informative — genuinely useful, and never the actual bar something is measured against.

contentSections.title: When advisory still matters in practice

contentSections.body: "It's only an advisory technique, so it's optional." True in the strict conformance sense — and a team that treats every advisory technique as dispensable ends up with a page that scrapes past AA and is still genuinely worse to use than it needed to be.

contentSections.question: A team asks: "If advisory techniques aren't required for conformance, why would we ever spend time on them?" What's the honest one-sentence answer?
contentSections.hint: What's the gap between "conforms to AA" and "is genuinely pleasant and low-effort to use"?
contentSections.answer: Because conformance is a floor, not a target — an interface can pass every mandatory AA criterion and still be exhausting to use, and advisory techniques are the W3C's own list of the specific, well-evidenced improvements that close that gap. Skipping all of them isn't a violation; it's a choice to stop at the legal minimum on purpose.

contentSections.scenario: A design system review turns up six items. Judge each one on whether skipping it puts a specific success criterion at risk of failing, versus whether it's purely a best-practice improvement with no citable criterion behind it.
contentSections.question: Select every item that is an advisory (best-practice, non-mandatory) technique rather than something a specific success criterion requires.

items.label: Limiting body text line length to roughly 80 characters for readability
Meeting 4.5:1 contrast on body text
Providing a text label alongside every icon-only button
Writing at a lower secondary-school reading level where the content allows it
Giving every interactive element a visible focus indicator
Slowing all page transition animations to reduce visual intensity, beyond what reduced-motion preferences require

explanation.linewidth: Advisory. WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) addresses line length as part of a broader visual-presentation criterion most sites don't target at that level, so this is best-practice guidance without a mandatory AA citation behind it for most contexts.
explanation.contrast: Not advisory — this is SC 1.4.3, a Level AA requirement with a specific measurable threshold, mandatory for most conformance claims.
explanation.iconlabel: Not advisory — an icon-only button with no accessible name fails SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value directly. This is often mistaken for a style preference; it's a hard requirement.
explanation.readinglevel: Advisory — SC 3.1.5 Reading Level exists at Level AAA and is one of the criteria WCAG itself flags as not achievable for all content types. Genuinely good practice, not a mandatory AA bar.
explanation.focusvisible: Not advisory — SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA) requires it directly, and WCAG 2.2 tightened this further with 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured.
explanation.animspeed: Advisory beyond the mandatory floor — SC 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions) is AAA, and the mandatory floor (2.2.2, 2.3.1) covers auto-playing and flashing content specifically, not general transition speed.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six are mandatory AA requirements with a specific citation; three are genuinely advisory. The distinction matters for how you write the finding — a mandatory item goes in the conformance section with a citation and a severity rating; an advisory item can still be worth recommending, framed honestly as "beyond the required baseline" rather than dressed up as a conformance failure it isn't.

contentSections.body: Advisory doesn't mean unimportant — it means uncited. Recommend it honestly as best practice, not as a conformance failure it isn't.

title: Citing the Right Criterion Instead of the Nearest One
description: The reflex citations — 4.1.2 for anything ARIA-shaped, 2.1.1 for anything keyboard-adjacent — and the habit that replaces them: naming the actual mechanism of the failure before reaching for a number.

learningObjectives.text: Identify common miscitation patterns and the reflex behind each
Cite the success criterion that actually governs a specific failure

contentSections.title: The nearest number is not the right number

contentSections.body: A reviewer cites 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value on almost every finding that involves a custom control, because it's the one they remember best. Half the time it's right. The other half, there's a more specific criterion sitting one line away in the spec that actually governs the defect.

contentSections.scenario: A custom toggle switch is built as a `<div>` with `role="switch"` and `aria-checked` correctly wired up — the accessible name, role and state are all exposed properly. The problem: it can only be activated by clicking with a mouse. There's no keydown handler at all, so it's entirely unreachable and unusable from a keyboard.
contentSections.question: What's the governing citation?

options.label: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value — the ARIA implementation is the issue
2.1.1 Keyboard — the control has no keyboard operability at all
1.3.1 Info and Relationships — the semantic structure is wrong

feedback.211: Correct. Name, role and value are all exposed properly here — that part is done right, which is exactly why the reflex citation (4.1.2, because it's a custom ARIA control) is wrong. The actual defect is that nothing in the implementation lets a keyboard user reach or activate it, which is precisely what 2.1.1 governs: all functionality operable through a keyboard interface.
feedback.412: 4.1.2 is the reflex for "custom control, must be an ARIA problem" — but 4.1.2 covers whether the control's name, role and state are correctly exposed to assistive technology, and this one's ARIA wiring is fine. The defect is somewhere else entirely: there's no keyboard handler.
feedback.131: 1.3.1 covers whether information and relationships conveyed visually are also conveyed programmatically (heading structure, form-label association, table headers). Nothing about this defect is a structure-versus-presentation mismatch — it's a missing interaction handler.

contentSections.concept: **Reflex citations happen when a criterion number gets associated with a category of control rather than with the specific mechanism of a specific failure.** "Custom control → 4.1.2" is a pattern-match, not an analysis. The fix is to ask, every time: what specifically is broken — is it that assistive tech can't determine what the control is (4.1.2), that it can't be operated by keyboard (2.1.1), that its state isn't announced when it changes (4.1.2 again, or a live-region gap under 4.1.3), or something else entirely? Naming the mechanism first, citation second, is the same discipline the previous module built the whole finding procedure around.

contentSections.body:
A short list of the reflex citations worth knowing by name, because they're common enough to catch yourself doing:

- **"It's a custom control" → always 4.1.2.** Frequently right, but check separately whether the *interaction* (keyboard, timing) also fails a different criterion.
- **"There's an image" → always 1.1.1.** True if the alt is missing or wrong; not the citation if the actual defect is that the image is decorative and unnecessarily focusable (that's a 2.1.1/4.1.2 pairing) or that its caption's contrast fails (1.4.3).
- **"Something with colour" → always 1.4.3 Contrast.** 1.4.1 (Use of Color) is a separate criterion — for when colour is the *only* way information is conveyed (a required field marked red with no other indicator), regardless of whether the contrast ratio itself is fine.
- **"Anything with focus" → always 2.4.7.** 2.4.3 (Focus Order) and 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured, WCAG 2.2) are both focus-adjacent and cover different mechanisms — order versus visibility versus whether the focused element is hidden behind other content.
A reflex citation is a pattern-match on the type of control, not an analysis of the actual mechanism that failed. Name the mechanism first.
The fix for reflex citation isn't memorising more criterion numbers. It's a two-question habit you can run in under ten seconds on anything you're about to cite.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order that actually produces an accurate citation, rather than the nearest familiar one.
steps: State the observed failure in plain language, with no criterion number attached yet
Ask: what specific mechanism is broken — exposure to assistive tech, keyboard operability, timing, visual presentation, structure, or something else
Search the success criteria under the matching guideline for the one whose exact wording matches the mechanism
Read that criterion's full text, including exceptions, before finalising
Check whether a second, distinct mechanism is also present and needs its own separate citation
contentSections.explanation:
The ordering that matters most is that the plain-language failure comes before any number does. Starting from a remembered criterion and looking for a matching defect is exactly backwards — it's the same mistake the previous module warned against at the level of the whole finding, applied here specifically to citation.

Step five is the one worth calling out on its own: a single defect often trips two mechanisms at once (the keyboard-inaccessible toggle from this lesson's concept-flow could *also* fail 4.1.2 if its `aria-checked` never updates on activation). Citing only the first one you find under-reports the defect.

contentSections.body: Name the mechanism in plain language before you reach for a number. The criterion should follow from the failure, never the other way round.

title: Practice — Citing the Governing Criterion
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where naming the right criterion stops being a lookup and becomes a reflex you can trust.

learningObjectives.text: Cite the governing success criterion for a range of specific defects at speed
Distinguish normative requirements from advisory best practice under time pressure

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing is timed and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Build Your Own Working WCAG Reference
description: Produce a personal reference for the twenty success criteria you'll cite most often — in your own words, with the exception clauses that actually matter, not a copy-paste of the spec.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the success criteria most relevant to your own reviewing work
Rewrite each criterion's requirement and key exceptions in plain, citable language

contentSections.body: Copying WCAG's own text into a cheat sheet doesn't make it faster to use — you'll still have to parse the same dense legal-standard prose under pressure, mid-audit. A reference in your own words, written once and understood completely, is faster every single time after that.

contentSections.title: Your working WCAG reference
contentSections.brief: You're about to spend a career citing WCAG success criteria under time pressure, mid-audit, without a chance to re-read the spec each time. This lab produces the document that removes that re-reading step: a plain-language reference for the twenty criteria you'll reach for constantly, in language you wrote and will actually remember.
contentSections.deliverable: A personal reference covering twenty success criteria: each one's number, level, a plain-language restatement of the requirement, its key exception(s) if any, and one real example of a pass and a fail.

stages.title: Choose your twenty
stages.instructions: Start from the criteria this module and the previous one named directly (1.1.1, 1.4.3, 2.1.1, 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 4.1.2, and others). Add criteria you expect to cite often given the kind of product you'll be reviewing. Don't aim for coverage of the whole spec — twenty is the number for a reason: it's what you can actually hold in working memory.
stages.checkpoint: You have exactly twenty named criteria, each with its official number and level (A/AA/AAA).

stages.title: Rewrite each requirement in your own words
stages.instructions: For each criterion, write the requirement the way you'd actually explain it to a developer in conversation — plain, specific, no legal hedging carried over from the spec's own phrasing. Include the exception clauses that change how the criterion applies (large text, incidental content, and so on) — leaving these out is the mistake this module's third lesson was built around.
stages.checkpoint: Every entry is written in your own words, not copied from the spec, and includes any exceptions that materially change how it's applied.

stages.title: Add one real pass and one real fail example per criterion
stages.instructions: For each of the twenty, write one concrete example that passes and one that fails — a specific number, a specific control, a specific piece of markup, drawn from something you've actually seen or can precisely imagine. "A button with alt text" is not specific enough; "a `<button>` with `aria-label="Close dialog"` and no visible text" is.
stages.checkpoint: Every criterion has one concrete pass example and one concrete fail example, both specific enough that someone else could tell which was which without your explanation.

rubric.criterion: Twenty criteria, correctly numbered and levelled
rubric.meets: Every entry has the correct official number and conformance level — check these against the spec, since getting them wrong defeats the reference's purpose.

rubric.criterion: Requirements are in your own words
rubric.meets: No entry is a direct copy of WCAG's or Understanding WCAG's phrasing — each reads like something you'd say out loud.

rubric.criterion: Exceptions are included where they matter
rubric.meets: Any criterion with a real exception clause (1.4.3, 1.1.1, and others) states it, not just the headline threshold.

rubric.criterion: Every entry has a concrete pass and fail example
rubric.meets: Both examples are specific — a real number, a real element — not a generic restatement of the rule.

rubric.criterion: It's usable under time pressure
rubric.meets: You could find and apply the right entry in under thirty seconds during a real review, without re-reading the spec.

contentSections.body: A reference you wrote yourself, in your own words, is one you'll actually reach for mid-audit. A copy of the spec is one more document to re-read.

title: Checkpoint — Reading WCAG Properly
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the previous one, and the module before that. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's citation discipline and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: Which layer of WCAG's structure is the one you cite in a finding?

options.label: The principle (e.g. Perceivable)
The success criterion (e.g. 1.1.1)
The guideline (e.g. 1.1 Text Alternatives)

questions.explanation: Success criteria are the only layer written as a testable pass/fail statement with a conformance level. Principles and guidelines organise the standard; they aren't citable on their own.

questions.from: This module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: A team uses an interaction pattern not documented in any WCAG technique, but it genuinely satisfies the criterion's actual text. Does it conform?

options.label: No — only documented techniques count
Yes — techniques are informative examples, not an exhaustive requirement
Only once the W3C adds a technique document for it

questions.explanation: Only the success criteria are normative. A novel approach that meets the criterion's actual wording meets the criterion, whether or not a technique document exists for it.

questions.from: This module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: Why is AAA conformance not recommended as a site-wide target?

options.label: It's simply too expensive for most organisations
WCAG itself states some AAA criteria can't be met for certain content types without changing what the content fundamentally is
AAA criteria are outdated and rarely tested by browsers

questions.explanation: This is WCAG's own stated position, not a cost argument — some AAA criteria (like sign-language interpretation for all audio) genuinely cannot be satisfied for every kind of content.

questions.from: This module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: A conformance claim says a checkout flow conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA. What does that claim NOT assert?

options.label: That every AA criterion is met within the checkout flow
That the entire website, beyond checkout, is covered
That the claim describes a specific point in time

questions.explanation: A conformance claim only covers the scope it explicitly states. The other two options describe things the claim genuinely does assert.

questions.from: This module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: A custom control has correct name, role and value exposed via ARIA, but no keyboard handler at all. What's the reflex miscitation, and what's correct?

options.label: Reflex: 4.1.2. Correct: 2.1.1 Keyboard, since the ARIA exposure is fine but nothing lets a keyboard reach or activate it
Reflex: 2.1.1. Correct: 4.1.2, since it's a custom control
Both citations are equally valid regardless of the actual mechanism

questions.explanation: "Custom control" pattern-matches to 4.1.2 by reflex, but the actual broken mechanism here is keyboard operability — a distinct criterion from whether the control's name and state are exposed correctly.

questions.from: Previous module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a barrier and an impairment, in this track's vocabulary?

options.label: A barrier is a fact about a design; an impairment is a fact about a body or mind
They're interchangeable terms for the same thing
A barrier is more severe than an impairment

questions.explanation: Impairment is a fact about a person. Barrier is a fact about the design. Disability is what happens when the two meet — and only the barrier is the reviewer's job to fix.

questions.from: Previous module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a fluctuating access need from a temporary one?

options.label: A temporary need resolves and stays resolved; a fluctuating one recurs unpredictably, indefinitely
Fluctuating needs are always more severe
There is no meaningful difference between the two

questions.explanation: A cast comes off and stays off. A fluctuating condition's bad day comes back on no fixed schedule, which is why the design fix has to hold indefinitely.

questions.from: Older module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: In the finding procedure from the first module of this track, what comes first?

options.label: The success criterion
The task the user was trying to complete
The severity rating

questions.explanation: Task, access method, where it stops, what they're left with, citation — in that order. Citation is last, not first, in both the original finding procedure and in this module's citation habit.

questions.from: Older module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Roughly what share of accessibility barriers does an automated scanner detect on a typical site?

options.label: About 30%, and the figure depends heavily on how you count
About 90%
Nearly all of them with a well-configured tool

questions.explanation: Somewhere in the 20-40% range. Scanners are near-complete on markup properties and structurally blind to meaning, layout and runtime behaviour.

questions.from: Older module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Which reader of an audit is most likely to read the scope statement first?

options.label: The developer fixing an individual ticket
A procurement reviewer comparing suppliers
Nobody — scope statements are rarely read

questions.explanation: Accessibility statements are self-declared, so a procurement reviewer's basis for trusting one is the evidence behind it — and that evidence is largely the scope statement.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Why a Company Is Asking for This Audit at All
description: The honest range of reasons an organisation commissions accessibility work — litigation, procurement pressure, a looming deadline, genuine conviction — and why naming the real trigger changes how you scope, not what you're honest about finding.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the common triggers that lead an organisation to commission an audit
Explain why the trigger should shape scope and priority without compromising rigor

contentSections.title: Legal exposure is usually the real trigger

contentSections.body: A company that has never once mentioned accessibility suddenly wants a full audit, fast, with a deadline in three weeks. Nobody explains why. It's worth asking — not to judge the answer, but because the honest answer usually changes what the audit needs to actually cover.

contentSections.scenario: A mid-size retailer's legal team emails, out of nowhere, asking for an urgent audit of their checkout flow and their homepage, "as soon as possible." No accessibility programme existed before this email.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely thing driving this request?

options.label: A sudden, spontaneous commitment to inclusive design
A demand letter or lawsuit naming those specific pages
A new hire who happens to care about accessibility

feedback.litigation: Statistically, yes — and the tell is the specificity: legal urgency, a short deadline, and pages named rather than "the whole site." This pattern is exactly what a demand letter or a filed lawsuit produces, since plaintiffs' counsel typically names specific pages and specific barriers they've already documented.
feedback.spontaneous: It happens, but it's the least common trigger by a wide margin, and it rarely produces this specific shape — urgent, legal-team-initiated, narrowly scoped to particular pages.
feedback.newhire: Possible, but a genuinely values-driven internal push usually comes with a longer runway and broader initial scope ("audit the whole product"), not urgent legal-team pressure on two named pages.

contentSections.concept:
**The honest range of triggers**, roughly in order of how often they actually show up: a demand letter or active litigation naming specific barriers; a procurement requirement from a public-sector or enterprise customer who requires a conformance claim before they'll sign; an approaching regulatory deadline (the European Accessibility Act's June 2025 compliance date drove a large wave of this kind of work); an internal risk or brand audit with no external pressure yet; and, genuinely but least frequently, leadership conviction with no external trigger at all.

None of these change what rigorous audit work looks like. What they change is scope and priority — and asking, directly, "what's driving this?" is a normal, professional question that gets you a better-scoped engagement, not a nosy one.

contentSections.body: Litigation, procurement pressure and looming deadlines are the most common real triggers, far more than sudden conviction. Naming the actual one gets you a better-scoped audit.

contentSections.title: The trigger shapes scope, not rigor

contentSections.body: A reviewer treats "why now" as background colour and scopes the audit exactly the way they'd scope any other. Three weeks later, opposing counsel's letter cites a specific carousel component the audit never looked at, because the audit was organised by page instead of by the flow the letter actually named.

contentSections.scenario: A retailer facing litigation over an inaccessible checkout hires an auditor. The auditor scopes broadly — homepage, product pages, checkout, account settings — spreading limited hours evenly across all four. The demand letter, which the auditor never asked to see, named three specific defects in the checkout flow's payment step.
contentSections.question: What went wrong with the scoping?

options.label: Nothing — broad coverage is always the more thorough choice
The audit didn't prioritise the exact area the actual legal exposure lives in, because nobody asked what the letter said
The auditor should have refused the engagement entirely, since it's litigation-driven

feedback.misaligned: Right. Spreading hours evenly across four areas sounds thorough and is actually a mismatch: the client's real, urgent need was deep, evidenced coverage of the three specific checkout defects named in the letter, with enough rigor that counsel could use the findings directly. A broad, shallow pass across the whole site serves a different kind of engagement — this one needed depth exactly where the exposure was, which required asking to see the letter before scoping anything.
feedback.nothingwrong: Breadth is the right call for a general accessibility programme audit. It's the wrong call when a specific, already-identified set of defects is the actual thing at stake — depth there is worth more than breadth everywhere.
feedback.refuse: Litigation-driven work is a completely normal and legitimate reason to commission an audit — refusing it wouldn't serve the client or the disabled users affected by the named defects, and it isn't what the mismatch here calls for.

contentSections.mechanism: **The trigger tells you where the real stakes are, and scoping without that information produces work that's technically thorough and practically useless for what the client actually needed.** This isn't a case for cutting corners elsewhere — it's a case for asking a direct, professional question early ("is there a specific letter, ticket, or requirement I should see before we finalise scope?") so the hours you have land where they matter most.

contentSections.body: One more thing worth naming plainly: knowing the trigger never changes what you're honest about finding. If a litigation-driven audit turns up a fourth defect the letter didn't mention, it goes in the report — the trigger shapes where you look first and how you prioritise limited hours, never what you report once you've looked.
Ask what's driving the engagement, early and directly. It changes where your hours go, never what you're willing to report.

title: European Requirements: EN 301 549 and the Accessibility Act
description: EN 301 549 covers more than the web, and two separate EU directives govern who has to comply and by when — the distinction that decides whether a given product is in scope at all.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what EN 301 549 covers beyond WCAG
Distinguish the Web Accessibility Directive's scope from the European Accessibility Act's

contentSections.body: A developer asks: "What's EN 301 549 — is it just WCAG with a European name?" Partly. It incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA by reference for web content, and then covers a whole category of things WCAG was never written to address.

**EN 301 549** is the EU's harmonised standard for ICT accessibility. For web content and mobile apps, Clause 9 incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA directly — so everything from the earlier module on WCAG structure applies unchanged when EN 301 549 is the governing requirement.

Where it goes further: EN 301 549 also covers **non-web ICT** — hardware (self-service kiosks, ATMs, ticket machines), software that isn't a web app, real-time text and video communication, and documents. A self-checkout kiosk's physical button size, screen height and card-reader placement are EN 301 549 concerns with no WCAG equivalent at all, because WCAG was written for content rendered in a browser, not for the geometry of a physical device.

contentSections.scenario: A transit authority deploys self-service ticket kiosks: a touchscreen running a web-based interface, in a physical enclosure with a card reader and a coin slot, mounted at a fixed height.
contentSections.question: Which of these needs a check that WCAG alone would never surface?

options.label: Whether the on-screen "Buy Ticket" button has sufficient contrast
Whether the kiosk's mounted height and reach distance are usable from a seated position
Whether the touchscreen's form fields have programmatic labels

feedback.height: Correct. Mounting height, reach distance, and physical control placement are hardware ergonomics requirements — squarely inside EN 301 549's scope for self-service terminals, and completely outside anything WCAG's success criteria address, because WCAG governs rendered content, not the physical enclosure it's displayed in.
feedback.contrast: This is a straightforward WCAG 1.4.3 check, fully covered by EN 301 549's Clause 9 incorporation of WCAG — no gap here.
feedback.labels: Also a standard WCAG check (1.3.1 / 4.1.2), covered the same way as any web form. Nothing hardware-specific about it.

contentSections.concept: **EN 301 549 is broader than WCAG on purpose**, because ICT procurement in the EU covers far more than websites — kiosks, ATMs, telecoms equipment, software that never touches a browser. A reviewer auditing purely web content under EN 301 549 is, in practice, auditing against WCAG 2.1 AA. A reviewer auditing a physical device needs the standard's other clauses — and needs to say plainly in the scope section which parts were and weren't covered, exactly as the earlier module on scope statements taught.

contentSections.body: EN 301 549 incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA for web content and goes further for hardware and non-web ICT. Know which part of the standard actually applies to what you're reviewing.

"We're an EU company, so we're covered by the Accessibility Act" is a sentence that might be true, false, or true starting on a different date than the person saying it thinks — because two separate EU directives govern this, with different scopes and different timelines.

contentSections.scenario: Four organisations, each asking whether EU accessibility law applies to them.
contentSections.question: Select every one where a specific EU directive (Web Accessibility Directive or European Accessibility Act) is very likely to apply, based on what's described.

items.label: A national tax authority's online filing portal
A private retail bank's mobile banking app
A single-location bakery's informational website, with no online ordering
An e-book retailer selling digital books to EU consumers

explanation.gov: The Web Accessibility Directive covers public-sector bodies directly — a national tax authority's portal is about as clear a case as exists.
explanation.bank: Banking services are one of the European Accessibility Act's named categories for private-sector coverage.
explanation.localshop: A purely informational site with no e-commerce transaction, from a business well outside the Act's named categories, is the case most likely to fall outside both directives — though "most likely" is doing real work in that sentence, and specifics (does it take bookings? does it process payments in any form?) matter.
explanation.ebook: E-books are one of the Accessibility Act's explicitly named categories.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the four are squarely covered; one sits in the genuinely uncertain territory these two directives leave outside their named scope. The practical lesson for a reviewer: don't answer "are we covered" from memory — check which directive's named categories the specific product and sector actually fall into, and flag genuine uncertainty rather than guessing confidently in either direction.

contentSections.body:
**The Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102)** covers public-sector websites and mobile apps — government agencies, public universities, publicly funded services. It requires conformance to EN 301 549, and it requires publishing an accessibility statement (the subject of the next lesson).

**The European Accessibility Act (Directive 2019/882)**, with obligations applying from 28 June 2025, covers specific categories of *private-sector* products and services: e-commerce, banking services, e-books, transport ticketing (including those kiosks), telecommunications, and a defined list of others. It does not cover every private business — a small local shop's website with no e-commerce function, for instance, generally sits outside its named categories, though national implementations vary and this is exactly the kind of question that needs actual legal counsel, not a course lesson.

A product can be covered by one, both, or neither, depending on who operates it and what it does — which is why "we're an EU company" alone doesn't answer the question.

The Web Accessibility Directive covers the public sector. The European Accessibility Act covers named private-sector categories from June 2025. Neither covers everything — check the actual scope, don't assume it.

title: US Requirements: the ADA and Section 508
description: The ADA has no explicit web-accessibility text at all, which is exactly why the case law that's grown up around it matters — and Section 508 covers a narrower, more explicit slice: federal agencies and what they buy.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish ADA Title II from Title III and what each actually requires for digital products
Explain what Section 508 covers and who it directly binds
Identify which US framework governs a specific organisation

contentSections.title: The ADA: two titles, two different pictures

contentSections.body: "Are we legally required to be accessible in the US?" is a harder question to answer honestly than the equivalent one in the EU, because the Americans with Disabilities Act predates the web by years and, for a large share of private business, still doesn't name it explicitly.

The ADA has two titles that matter here, and they're in very different positions:

**Title II** covers state and local government. A 2024 Department of Justice rule made the requirement explicit for the first time: state and local government websites and mobile apps must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, on a phased timeline based on the size of the population served. This is about as clear as US accessibility law gets.

**Title III** covers private businesses that are "places of public accommodation" — a phrase written in 1990 to mean physical spaces, long before anyone was thinking about websites. There is still no federal regulation formally extending Title III to the web the way the 2024 rule did for Title II. What exists instead is a large and fairly consistent body of case law: courts across multiple circuits have repeatedly held that a business's website or app is covered by Title III when it's closely tied to the goods or services of a physical or online business, and have routinely pointed to WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 AA as the practical benchmark for what accessible means, without that benchmark being written into a federal regulation.

contentSections.scenario: A private, US-only e-commerce retailer with no physical stores asks whether Title III really applies to them, since they're not a "place" in the way a shop or a restaurant is.
contentSections.question: What's the accurate, honest answer?

options.label: No — Title III only covers physical locations, full stop

There's no explicit federal regulation naming e-commerce sites, but courts have repeatedly found online-only retailers covered under Title III, so the real-world exposure is significant despite the regulatory gap
Yes — a 2024 DOJ rule explicitly requires it, the same as Title II

feedback.risk: This is the honest, useful answer — genuinely uncertain in the strict regulatory sense, and genuinely risky in practice, because the case law has trended toward coverage even without a formal rule. Telling a client "no explicit law applies" would be technically arguable and practically misleading, given the actual litigation pattern.
feedback.no: This misses the entire body of case law that's developed specifically because the statute's own text is ambiguous on this point. "No regulation says so explicitly" is not the same claim as "no real legal risk exists."
feedback.yesrule: The 2024 DOJ rule is specifically about Title II (state and local government) — it did not extend the same explicit WCAG requirement to Title III private businesses. Conflating the two overstates how settled Title III actually is.

contentSections.concept: **Title II is now explicit and specific (WCAG 2.1 AA, phased deadlines). Title III is genuinely murkier at the regulatory level and genuinely risky at the practical level**, because of consistent case law rather than a written rule. A reviewer's job isn't to resolve that legal uncertainty — it's to know it exists, communicate it honestly to a client rather than overstating settled law in either direction, and point them toward counsel for anything contract- or litigation-shaped. This lesson is not legal advice; it's the map of which conversations need a lawyer.

contentSections.body: Title II is explicit: WCAG 2.1 AA, phased deadlines, state and local government. Title III is regulatorily murkier and practically risky — case law, not a rule, is doing the work.

A startup selling software to a federal agency gets asked, mid-procurement, for something called a VPAT. Nobody on the team has heard the term before, and the deal is stuck until someone produces one.

contentSections.problem: You're asked which US framework governs three different organisations. Work through each.

steps.label: A state department of motor vehicles' website
steps.work: ADA Title II — state government, so the 2024 DOJ rule applies directly: WCAG 2.1 AA, on the phased deadline for their population size.
steps.why: State and local government is the cleanest, most explicit case in US accessibility law right now.

steps.label: A private SaaS company selling project-management software directly to the public, with no government contracts
steps.work: ADA Title III, in the case-law sense described in the previous pod — no formal federal rule, but real litigation exposure, with WCAG 2.1 AA as the de facto benchmark courts point to.
steps.why: No government relationship means Section 508 doesn't apply at all; the relevant framework is the murkier, case-law-driven Title III picture.

steps.label: That same SaaS company, once it signs a contract to sell the software to a federal agency
steps.work: Section 508 procurement requirements kick in for that specific sale — the agency will likely require a VPAT/ACR, and the product needs to actually meet WCAG 2.0/2.1 AA, not just claim to on paper.
steps.why: Section 508 attaches to the procurement relationship specifically. The same company can be outside its scope for direct consumer sales and squarely inside it the moment a federal contract exists.

faded.problem: Fourth case: a private university that receives federal research funding but is not a public institution.

blanks.prompt: Which framework most directly governs, given federal funding is involved?
blanks.why: Section 504 (a sibling provision to 508, easy to confuse with it) prohibits disability discrimination by any recipient of federal financial assistance — which is the hook that pulls federally funded private institutions into accessibility obligations distinct from Title II or III.

blanks.prompt: Is this the same provision as Section 508?
blanks.why: 508 governs federal agencies' own procurement and ICT. 504 governs recipients of federal funding more broadly, including many private universities and hospitals. The numbers are close and the confusion is common — worth getting right.

contentSections.procedure: **Ask what kind of organisation it is, and what its relationship to government is** — state/local government (Title II), private with no government tie (Title III, case-law driven), selling to federal agencies (Section 508), or receiving federal funding (Section 504). Four different questions, four different answers, and getting the org type right is most of the work.

contentSections.body:
**Section 508** of the Rehabilitation Act covers a narrower, more explicit slice than the ADA: US federal agencies' own information and communications technology, and — the part that reaches private companies — what those agencies procure. Since the 2017 ICT Final Rule, Section 508 incorporates WCAG 2.0 Level AA as its technical standard (later guidance references 2.1; check the current rule text for a specific procurement, since this is exactly the kind of detail that shifts).

The practical document that shows up constantly here is the **VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template)** — a standardised form a vendor fills out, criterion by criterion, describing how their product conforms. A completed VPAT is called an ACR (Accessibility Conformance Report). Federal buyers routinely require one before purchasing software, which is why sales teams sometimes fill one out quickly, optimistically, and without engineering input — a pattern worth watching for specifically, because a VPAT's claims are exactly the kind of thing an audit can be asked to verify.
Section 508 governs federal ICT and procurement, explicitly requiring WCAG conformance and often a VPAT/ACR. It's the narrowest of the frameworks in scope and the most explicit in what it demands.

title: Accessibility Statements and What Makes One Dishonest
description: What a genuine accessibility statement has to contain, why 'fully accessible' is close to always a lie, and how to tell a defensible disproportionate-burden claim from an excuse.

learningObjectives.text: Name the required contents of a genuine accessibility statement
Identify claims in a statement that overstate what an audit would actually support
Distinguish a defensible disproportionate-burden claim from an unjustified excuse

contentSections.body: "This website is fully accessible to all users." Almost nothing that's ever shipped could honestly say that — not because teams don't try, but because "fully" and "all" are claims a single sentence can't actually carry.

A genuine accessibility statement, under the Web Accessibility Directive's model (increasingly the template private organisations follow too, whether or not they're legally required to), states: the current **compliance status** against a named standard (e.g. "partially conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA"); the **specific non-accessible content**, named, with the reason it isn't accessible; a **disproportionate burden justification** if any content is excluded on that basis, with the reasoning documented, not just asserted; a **feedback mechanism** for users to report barriers; and a **preparation and review date**, since a statement that never gets updated stops being true the moment anything on the site changes.

The honest version is almost always "partially conforms," named specifically, dated. "Fully accessible" is the sentence a genuine statement almost never contains, because it's a claim about a moving target that nobody can verify indefinitely.

contentSections.code:
Accessibility Statement

This website is fully accessible and meets all
WCAG 2.1 AA requirements. We are committed to
accessibility for all our users.

Last updated: 2019
contentSections.question: This statement has more than one problem. Which is the most serious?

options.label: It uses "fully accessible," an absolute claim, with no named exceptions or scope
It's too short — a good statement needs more paragraphs
It should mention the company's diversity policy

feedback.absolute: Correct, and it compounds with the second problem hiding in plain sight: a five-year-old date on a claim this absolute means either nothing has changed on the site since 2019 (extremely unlikely) or the statement has been silently false for years without anyone checking. "Fully accessible" with no named exceptions is very rarely a defensible claim for anything of real complexity, and a stale date is the tell that nobody's actually re-verifying it.
feedback.length: Length isn't the defect — a short, honest, specific statement ("partially conforms; known issues X and Y; last reviewed March 2026") beats a long vague one every time. The problem is what it claims, not how much space it takes to claim it.
feedback.diversity: Not what an accessibility statement is for — it's a technical compliance and feedback document, not a values statement. Including one doesn't fix the substantive problems here.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Fully accessible" plus a stale date is the exact pattern a procurement reviewer or opposing counsel is trained to flag on sight — it reads as either untested or untrue, and either reading is bad for the organisation making the claim. The lesson from the earlier module on procurement applies directly here: an unverified absolute claim is worth less than a modest, specific, dated one, because the modest one is checkable and survives scrutiny.

contentSections.body: A genuine statement names specific gaps, dates itself, and offers a feedback route. "Fully accessible," undated, with nothing named, is close to always false.

contentSections.title: Disproportionate burden: a documented claim, not an excuse

contentSections.body: A team excludes a legacy PDF archive from their accessibility work with one line: "remediating this would be disproportionate." That might be true. It might also be the sentence that gets written whenever something is inconvenient — and the difference is entirely in what comes after it.

contentSections.scenario: A public university claims disproportionate burden to avoid remediating twelve years of archived lecture recordings with no captions — roughly 40,000 hours of video, uploaded before any captioning workflow existed, most of it rarely accessed. Their statement's justification is one sentence: "Captioning this archive is not feasible."
contentSections.question: Is this a defensible disproportionate-burden claim as written?

options.label: Yes — 40,000 hours is self-evidently too much to caption

No — the volume might genuinely support the claim, but the statement doesn't document the actual reasoning (cost estimate, resources available, usage data, alternatives considered) that a defensible claim requires
No — disproportionate burden can never apply to video content

feedback.nounsupported: Right, and the distinction matters: the underlying claim might well be legitimate — 40,000 hours of low-traffic archival video is a real, large number, and a documented, reasoned exclusion (cost estimate against the institution's actual resources, usage data showing low demand, a stated plan for captioning new uploads going forward, and an alternative like captioning-on-request for anyone who asks) would likely be defensible. "Not feasible," with none of that reasoning shown, is an assertion, not a documented justification — and it's indistinguishable, on the page, from an excuse.
feedback.yesobvious: The scale genuinely might support an eventual burden claim — the problem here is that scale alone, asserted without any actual reasoning shown, isn't what a defensible claim looks like. "Self-evident" is doing the work a documented cost-benefit analysis is supposed to do.
feedback.nevervideo: Disproportionate burden isn't categorically barred for any content type — it's a documented, case-by-case justification available across content types, evaluated on the actual facts, not ruled out by the medium.

contentSections.mechanism: **A disproportionate burden claim has to show its work**: what remediation would cost, weighed against the organisation's actual resources and the benefit to actual users, with alternatives considered (partial remediation, remediation on request, a phased plan for new content even where the backlog stays excluded). A one-sentence assertion with no reasoning shown is the exact shape of both a legitimate claim that was written lazily and an illegitimate excuse — which is precisely why reviewers should treat an unsupported claim as a finding in itself, regardless of whether the underlying exclusion turns out to be reasonable.

contentSections.body: A disproportionate burden claim needs documented reasoning — cost, resources, usage, alternatives considered — not just the sentence asserting it. An unsupported claim is a finding, whatever the underlying facts turn out to be.

title: Procurement: Where Accessibility Gets Decided Before Design
description: The VPAT/ACR document that decides whether software gets bought, who fills it out, and why validating one against real evidence is some of the highest-leverage reviewing you'll ever do.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a VPAT/ACR is and its role in procurement
Judge whether a VPAT's claims are supported by real evidence
Handle a request to validate a VPAT before a contract is signed

contentSections.title: The document that decides the sale

contentSections.body: A public-sector RFP requires a completed VPAT before a vendor can even bid. Sales fills it out over an afternoon, mostly marking "Supports" because that's what sells the deal. Nobody in engineering ever sees the document — and it's the document the buyer's whole accessibility due diligence rests on.

A **VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template)** is a standardised reporting format, developed by the Information Technology Industry Council, where a vendor states — criterion by criterion, usually against WCAG or Section 508's technical requirements — whether their product Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, or is Not Applicable for each. A completed VPAT is called an **ACR (Accessibility Conformance Report)**.

It's self-reported, with no independent verification built into the process — which is precisely the procurement problem the earlier module's lesson on accessibility statements described, applied to a different document. A buyer's whole decision can rest on a document nobody outside sales has checked against the actual product.

contentSections.scenario: A vendor's VPAT claims "Supports" for SC 2.1.1 Keyboard. During a live demo, a procurement reviewer tries operating the product's core scheduling feature with the mouse unplugged and finds a drag-and-drop calendar entry with no keyboard alternative at all.
contentSections.question: What's the appropriate response to this gap?

options.label: Assume the VPAT is describing a different part of the product, and move on
Flag the specific discrepancy — the claimed conformance and the observed behaviour — and ask the vendor to either fix it or correct the VPAT
Reject the vendor outright without further conversation

feedback.flag: Right. This is exactly the kind of specific, evidenced discrepancy a procurement review is for — name the claim, name the observed contradiction, and give the vendor a chance to respond, either by fixing the actual defect or by correcting an inaccurate document. Most VPAT errors come from an unverified sales-team claim rather than deliberate deception, and a direct, specific challenge is the useful next step either way.
feedback.assume: Explaining away a specific, reproducible contradiction is exactly the failure mode that lets an inaccurate VPAT go unchallenged — the whole point of testing a claim is to trust what you observed over what the document asserts.
feedback.reject: One unverified claim doesn't automatically mean the whole VPAT is worthless — it might be an isolated gap in an otherwise accurate document, or it might not be. Reject-without-conversation skips the step that would actually tell you which.

contentSections.concept: **A VPAT is a claim, not evidence.** Validating one is straightforward, high-leverage reviewing: pick a sample of the criteria marked "Supports," test them directly against the actual product, and treat every mismatch as a specific, named discrepancy to raise — not proof the whole document is fraudulent, and not something to quietly let slide either.

contentSections.body: A VPAT is self-reported and rarely independently checked before it decides a purchase. Testing a sample of its claims against the real product is some of the highest-leverage work a reviewer can do.

contentSections.title: Being the one asked to validate it
