Sign-off, three days before the contract closes
contentSections.opening: Procurement asks you to "sanity-check" a vendor's VPAT before a six-figure contract closes in three days. The VPAT claims full WCAG 2.1 AA support. You have limited access — a sandbox account, no source code, and three days.

start.situation: Three days is not enough time to verify all ~50 relevant success criteria against a product you've never used, from a sandbox account with limited permissions.
start.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Attempt a full conformance audit in the time available
choices.consequence: You run out of time on day two, having covered maybe a third of the criteria at real depth, and have to report an incomplete picture as though it were thorough.

choices.label: Tell procurement it can't be meaningfully done in three days and decline
choices.consequence: Technically true, and it leaves them with nothing at all going into a contract signing they can't delay.

choices.label: Propose a scoped, honest alternative: a risk-weighted sample of the highest-stakes criteria and flows, clearly labelled as a spot-check, not a full audit
choices.consequence: You test keyboard operability, screen reader basics, and contrast across the three core workflows the buyer actually plans to use daily — the highest-value ten hours available, explicitly scoped as such.

findings.situation: You find two real discrepancies: a claimed-Supports criterion that fails on the main dashboard, and one that genuinely passes. You have half a day left to report.
findings.question: How do you write it up?

choices.label: Report exactly what you tested, what you found, and what remains genuinely unverified
choices.consequence: Procurement gets a scoped, honest spot-check: two concrete findings, a clear statement of what wasn't covered, and enough evidence to negotiate specific contract terms — remediation timelines tied to the named gaps — rather than either blind trust or a stalled deal.

rushed.summary: An incomplete audit gets reported without its incompleteness stated clearly, which is worse for the buyer than an honest spot-check would have been — they now believe they have more assurance than they do.
rushed.lesson: The wrong response to too little time is rarely to compress a full audit into it. A scoped, clearly-labelled spot-check that's honest about its limits gives the buyer something real to act on; a rushed full audit that quietly cuts corners gives them false confidence, which is worse than no audit at all.

unhelpful.summary: Technically correct, and it leaves the buyer with nothing at all going into a six-figure decision they can't postpone.
unhelpful.lesson: "Can't be done properly in the time available" is true and also not the end of the useful conversation — a scoped, honest partial check is real information a full refusal doesn't provide, as long as its limits are stated clearly.

resolved.summary: The buyer signs with two named gaps and remediation timelines written into the contract, plus an honest statement of what was and wasn't verified.
resolved.lesson: The move that worked was proposing the honest, scoped alternative before starting, not after running out of time — naming the constraint up front let everyone agree on what "done" meant, which is what made the three-day version actually useful instead of either falsely reassuring or useless.

contentSections.body: When there isn't time for a full audit, a scoped, honestly-labelled spot-check beats both a rushed full audit and a flat refusal — as long as its limits are stated as clearly as its findings.

title: Practice — Which Requirement Governs
description: Seven drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where naming the governing framework stops being a lookup.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the governing legal requirement for a range of specific scenarios
Evaluate accessibility statements and VPAT claims for what they actually support

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing is timed and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Review a Real Accessibility Statement Against Its Product
description: Take a published accessibility statement and the product it describes, and name every claim in the statement that the product doesn't actually support — the exact skill the previous module's lesson on procurement rewards.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a published accessibility statement's claims against a real product
Produce a review naming every unsupported claim with evidence

contentSections.body: A statement is a claim until someone checks it. This lab is the checking — find a real, published accessibility statement, and hold it up against the actual product it describes.

contentSections.title: Statement versus product
contentSections.brief: Find a real, publicly published accessibility statement — a government agency, a bank, a retailer, any organisation that has one online (searching "[organisation] accessibility statement" usually finds it quickly). You are producing the review a sceptical procurement officer or journalist would do: for each specific claim the statement makes, check it against the actual product and say plainly whether it holds up.
contentSections.deliverable: A review naming every specific, checkable claim in the statement, whether it holds up against direct testing, and the evidence either way.

stages.title: Read the statement and extract every checkable claim
stages.instructions: List every specific, testable assertion the statement makes — a conformance level, a named exception, a feature claim ("all videos are captioned"), a date. Ignore vague, unfalsifiable language for now ("we care about accessibility") — you can't check what isn't checkable, and that's worth noting separately.
stages.checkpoint: You have a list of specific, testable claims extracted from the statement's actual text.

stages.title: Test the highest-stakes claims directly
stages.instructions: Pick the three or four claims that would matter most if false (a core-flow conformance claim beats a footer-link claim) and test them yourself — keyboard-only, a screen reader if you have one available, contrast measurement, whatever the claim calls for. Note exactly what you did and what you found.
stages.checkpoint: Each tested claim has a specific method and a specific, evidenced result, not an impression.

stages.title: Write the review
stages.instructions: For each claim: quote it, state what you tested, state whether it holds up, and — if it doesn't — name the specific defect the way this track's finding procedure teaches (task, access method, where it stops). Note the statement's date and whether that date is plausible given what you found.
stages.checkpoint: Every claim in your review has a verdict and evidence behind it, and the write-up follows the finding procedure from earlier in this track.

rubric.criterion: Claims are extracted precisely from the statement's own text
rubric.meets: Each claim is quoted or closely paraphrased, not invented or assumed.

rubric.criterion: Testing is real, not assumed
rubric.meets: At least three claims were actually tested (keyboard, screen reader, contrast tool, or direct inspection), with the method stated.

rubric.criterion: Verdicts are evidenced
rubric.meets: Every verdict — holds up or doesn't — has a specific observation behind it, not a general impression.

rubric.criterion: Unsupported claims are written as findings, not accusations
rubric.meets: Follows the task/access-method/where-it-stops procedure rather than accusing the organisation of dishonesty.

rubric.criterion: The statement's date is evaluated
rubric.meets: States whether the date is plausible given what testing found, and why.

contentSections.body: An accessibility statement is a claim, not evidence. Checking it against the real product is a genuinely useful skill for exactly the procurement moments this module covers.

title: Checkpoint — The Law Behind the Standard
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the previous one, and modules before that. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's legal-framework distinctions and earlier modules' core content without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — The Law Behind the Standard

questions.from: This module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: What's the single most common real trigger for an organisation suddenly commissioning an accessibility audit?

options.label: Spontaneous leadership conviction
Litigation, procurement pressure, or a regulatory deadline
A new hire's personal interest

questions.explanation: These three are, statistically, far more common than spontaneous conviction — and knowing which one is driving an engagement changes scope and priority, never rigor.

questions.from: This module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: What does EN 301 549 cover that WCAG alone does not?

options.label: Nothing — it's identical to WCAG
Non-web ICT: hardware, kiosks, real-time communication, documents
Only mobile apps, not desktop software

questions.explanation: EN 301 549 incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA for web content and goes further, covering hardware ergonomics and other non-web ICT that WCAG was never written to address.

questions.from: This module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: Which EU directive covers public-sector websites specifically?

options.label: The Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102)
The European Accessibility Act (2019/882)
Neither — the EU has no directive covering the public sector

questions.explanation: The Web Accessibility Directive covers public-sector bodies. The European Accessibility Act covers named private-sector categories from June 2025 — two different directives with two different scopes.

questions.from: This module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: Why is ADA Title III's application to websites described as "murkier" than Title II's?

options.label: There's no formal federal regulation extending Title III explicitly to the web, unlike the 2024 rule for Title II — coverage instead rests on a consistent body of case law
Title III doesn't apply to any digital products at all
Title III was repealed

questions.explanation: Title II got an explicit 2024 DOJ rule (WCAG 2.1 AA, phased deadlines). Title III has no equivalent formal rule — the real-world exposure comes from courts, not a regulation.

questions.from: This module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: What is a VPAT/ACR?

options.label: An independently audited certification
A self-reported, standardised conformance document a vendor fills out, often used in procurement
A legal requirement only for EU companies

questions.explanation: A VPAT (completed version: ACR) is self-reported with no independent verification built in — which is exactly why testing a sample of its claims against the real product is high-leverage reviewing.

questions.from: Previous module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: Which layer of WCAG's structure is the one you cite in a finding?

options.label: The principle
The success criterion
The guideline

questions.explanation: Success criteria are the only testable, citable layer — principles and guidelines organise the standard but aren't themselves checkable.

questions.from: Previous module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: Why is AAA conformance not recommended as a site-wide target?

options.label: WCAG itself states some AAA criteria can't be met for all content types
AAA criteria are deprecated
It's purely a cost argument

questions.explanation: This is WCAG's own stated position — not a cost argument, a genuine achievability limit for certain content types.

questions.from: Older module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a barrier and an impairment, in this track's vocabulary?

options.label: A barrier is a fact about a design; an impairment is a fact about a body or mind
They're interchangeable
A barrier is always caused by an impairment

questions.explanation: Impairment is a fact about a person. Barrier is a fact about a design. Only the barrier is yours to fix.

questions.from: Older module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: In the finding procedure, what comes first?

options.label: The success criterion or legal citation
The task the user was trying to complete
The severity rating

questions.explanation: Task, access method, where it stops, what they're left with, citation — the same ordering this module applied to legal citations, not just WCAG ones.

questions.from: Older module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: Roughly what share of accessibility barriers does an automated scanner detect on a typical site?

options.label: About 30%, and the figure depends heavily on how you count
About 90%
Essentially all of them with the right tool

questions.explanation: Somewhere in the 20-40% range — scanners are near-complete on markup properties and structurally blind to meaning, layout and runtime behaviour.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Running axe, Lighthouse and a Browser Inspector
description: Four tools that do genuinely different jobs, three of them fully free with no catch — and the one skill underneath all of them: reading a computed accessible name directly in the browser's own inspector.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what axe, Lighthouse, WAVE and a browser's accessibility inspector are each for
State what each tool costs and what happens without a paid tier
Read a computed accessible name directly from the browser's accessibility tree

contentSections.body: Someone asks, "which accessibility scanner should I use, axe or Lighthouse or WAVE?" as though the answer picks one winner. They do genuinely different jobs, and the useful answer is usually "more than one, for different moments."

contentSections.scenario: You're mid-development, adding a new modal component, and want a fast sanity check before opening a PR — no client in the room, no report to produce, just "did I obviously break something."
contentSections.question: Which tool fits this moment best?

options.label: axe-core, run in the browser devtools extension or as a test assertion
A full manual audit with a screen reader
WAVE's visual overlay, screen-shared with a client

feedback.axe: Right fit. axe-core is fast, free, and built for exactly this — a quick, automated pass that catches markup-level regressions (missing labels, invalid ARIA, contrast) before anything ships. It's also the ruleset several other tools, including Lighthouse's accessibility category, build on underneath.
feedback.manual: A manual pass is the right tool eventually — for the finished component, or for anything the automated layer structurally can't see (this whole module's subject). It's overkill and too slow for "did I obviously break something" on a component still in progress.
feedback.wave: WAVE's visual overlay is genuinely good for a specific audience — someone who wants to *see* problems marked directly on the rendered page, which makes it excellent for client conversations. It's not the fastest fit for a solo mid-development sanity check.

contentSections.concept:
**Four tools, four different strengths:**

- **axe-core** (Deque, open source, free) — the rule engine most other tools build on. Fast, scriptable, embeds directly into test suites (Cypress, Playwright, Jest).
- **Lighthouse** (Google, built into Chrome DevTools, free) — convenient because it's already there in every Chrome install; its accessibility category runs a subset of axe's rules and produces a single score, useful as a quick signal, not a substitute for the full ruleset.
- **WAVE** (WebAIM, free browser extension; a paid API exists for bulk/automated use) — marks issues directly on the rendered page visually, which makes it unusually good for explaining a finding to someone non-technical.
- **The browser's own accessibility inspector** (built into every modern browser's devtools, always free) — shows the actual computed accessibility tree: name, role, value, state, for any element you select. This is the tool underneath all the others, and the one covered in the second half of this lesson.

Worth stating plainly, because the architecture this course teaches insists on it: **every one of these four has a genuinely free, fully functional path.** Paid tiers exist (Deque's axe DevTools Pro, Siteimprove, Level Access) and add site-wide crawling, monitoring and reporting dashboards at real ongoing subscription cost — valuable at scale, and never required to do real, rigorous manual and automated review. If a client's budget for a paid platform disappears, none of this module's skills disappear with it.

contentSections.body: axe for fast automated checks, Lighthouse for a quick built-in signal, WAVE for visual client conversations, the browser inspector for the ground truth underneath all three. All four have a real, sufficient free tier.

A scan says a button has an accessible name. Whose word are you taking for that? The browser's own accessibility inspector shows you the actual computed name — no tool's summary in between, no trusting a report.

contentSections.problem: Chrome DevTools, Elements panel, Accessibility pane. You select a button: `<button aria-label="Close"><svg>...</svg></button>`. Determine what its computed accessible name will be, and why.

steps.label: Check for aria-labelledby first
steps.why: The accessible name computation has a strict precedence order, and aria-labelledby sits at the top of it — checking it first, even when you suspect it's absent, builds the habit that catches the cases where it's present and overriding something else silently.

steps.label: Check for aria-label next
steps.why: aria-label is the second-highest precedence source. Once found, the computation stops here — nothing lower in the order gets consulted.

steps.label: State the computed name
steps.work: "Close" — sourced entirely from the aria-label attribute. The SVG's contents (even if they had internal text) are irrelevant once aria-label is present.
steps.why: This is exactly what the Accessibility pane's "Computed Properties" section will show directly — Name: "Close", Source: aria-label. No inference required; the browser did the computation and is showing its answer.

faded.problem: Second element, same panel: ``, where `.visually-hidden` is off-screen but present in the DOM and not `aria-hidden`.

blanks.prompt: Is there an aria-label or aria-labelledby here?
blanks.why: Neither of the two highest-precedence sources is present on this button, so the computation has to continue further down the order.

blanks.prompt: What supplies the accessible name instead?
blanks.answer: the visible text content, including the visually-hidden span
blanks.why: With no ARIA naming attribute present, the browser falls back to the element's text content — and visually-hidden (off-screen, but not aria-hidden or display:none) text is still part of that content, which is exactly the pattern used to give icon buttons a name that's readable by screen readers and invisible on screen.

blanks.prompt: What would the computed name be?
blanks.why: This is the whole point of the visually-hidden-span pattern — a name every assistive technology reads, that a sighted user never sees, achieved through ordinary text content rather than an ARIA attribute.

contentSections.procedure: **Check aria-labelledby → check aria-label → fall back to text content (including visually-hidden text) → fall back to other sources (title attribute, placeholder, as a last resort).** This is the actual precedence order browsers implement, and the inspector's Accessibility pane shows you the result of running it — trust that over a scan's summary line every time you can check it directly.

contentSections.body: The browser's own accessibility inspector shows the actual computed name, role and value — no summarising tool in between. It's the ground truth every scanner is trying to approximate.

title: The Share of Real Barriers a Scanner Can Detect
description: Which WCAG criteria are actually automatable, why that share has a hard ceiling no tool improvement will raise, and why the same page can score very differently across different scanners.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the structural reason only a bounded share of WCAG is automatable
Classify a success criterion as fully, partially or not automatable
Explain why two scanners can produce different results on the same page

contentSections.title: The ceiling is structural, not a tooling gap

contentSections.body: "Once the tools get better, they'll catch everything." This sentence assumes the current gap is a limitation of today's software. It isn't — it's a limitation of what a static analysis of markup can, in principle, ever determine, and no future version of any tool changes that.

contentSections.scenario: Two success criteria, side by side. **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)**: compare two colour values, compute a ratio, check it against a threshold. **2.4.6 Headings and Labels**: headings and labels describe the topic or purpose of the content they introduce.
contentSections.question: Which of these two criteria is a scanner structurally capable of fully checking?

options.label: 1.4.3, because it's a computation on values already present in the markup
2.4.6, because headings are easy to find in the DOM
Both, equally

feedback.1.4.3: Correct. Contrast is arithmetic — two colour values are present in the rendered styles, the ratio is a deterministic calculation, and the threshold is a fixed number. Nothing about it requires understanding what anything means.
feedback.2.4.6: A scanner can confirm a heading element exists, even confirm it isn't empty. It cannot determine whether "Section 3" or "More Info" actually describes the content that follows — that's a judgement about meaning, which is exactly the category no static analysis can perform.
feedback.both: The two criteria aren't remotely equivalent in this respect — one is a closed computation, the other requires understanding language and intent, which is a categorically different kind of problem.

contentSections.concept: **The dividing line is whether checking the criterion requires computation on values already in the markup, or requires understanding what something means.** Contrast, duplicate IDs, invalid ARIA attribute values, missing `alt` — all closed computations. Whether alt text is *accurate*, whether a heading *describes* what follows, whether tab order *matches* reading order, whether an error message *helps* — all require a model of meaning or intent that markup analysis doesn't have access to, and this is true of any static analysis, however sophisticated, not a gap specific to today's tools.

contentSections.scenario: Accessibility researchers and tool vendors have repeatedly tried to estimate what share of WCAG 2.x's success criteria are fully automatable — checkable with no human judgement at all.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of WCAG's Level A and AA success criteria are fully, reliably automatable?
contentSections.actualValue: roughly a fifth to a third
contentSections.explanation: Estimates vary by methodology and by how strictly "fully automatable" is defined, but they cluster in the 20-35% range — a minority, and a structural one, not a temporary one. The rest split between **partially automatable** (a scanner can flag a candidate for human review — "this heading exists, a human should confirm it makes sense" — without settling the question) and **not automatable at all** (meaningful sequence, purpose of link in context, cognitive load — nothing in the markup a scanner can even approximate). The earlier estimate from this track's very first module — that scanners catch roughly 30% of real-world barrier *instances* on a typical site — is a related but distinct number: that one's about instances found on real pages; this one's about which criteria could ever be checked by a machine in principle.

contentSections.body: Only a minority of WCAG's criteria are fully automatable, and the reason is structural — meaning and intent aren't things a markup analysis can access, at any level of tool sophistication.

contentSections.title: Why the same page scores differently

contentSections.body: A client shows you two numbers for the same page: Lighthouse says 96 out of 100. axe found 14 violations. They ask which one is right, as if the two numbers were supposed to agree.

contentSections.scenario: The same production page, scanned within the same hour: Lighthouse's accessibility category scores 96/100. Running the full axe-core ruleset against the same URL turns up 14 distinct violations, several at the "serious" level.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely reason these disagree so sharply?

options.label: One of the two tools is simply broken
Lighthouse runs a smaller subset of axe's rules and weights them into a single score differently than axe's own full report lists raw violations
The page changed between the two scans

feedback.subset: Right. Lighthouse's accessibility audit runs a curated subset of axe-core's rules — not the full ruleset — and converts the result into a single weighted score rather than a flat violation list. A page can score well on that subset while still tripping violations on rules Lighthouse doesn't run at all, or on rules axe weights differently. Neither tool is wrong; they're measuring overlapping but different things and presenting the result in different formats.
feedback.broken: Both tools are very likely working correctly. This is the trap of assuming disagreement means malfunction, when the actual cause is that the two tools were never claiming to check the same thing in the same way.
feedback.changed: Possible in principle, but not the likely explanation for a same-hour comparison, and it's not the structural reason this disagreement shows up constantly across completely unrelated pages and tools.

contentSections.mechanism: **Different tools implement different subsets of rules, at different strictness, presented in different formats — a single score, a violation count, a pass/fail per criterion.** None of that is a bug in either tool; it's a consequence of each one making its own choices about coverage and presentation. The practical implication for a reviewer: never present a single tool's score as *the* accessibility status of a page, and when a client asks which number is right, the honest answer is that both are partial, non-identical views of the same limited, automatable slice.

contentSections.body: Different tools run different rule subsets and present results differently. Disagreement between two clean-looking scores isn't a malfunction — it's two partial views of the same bounded, automatable slice.

title: False Positives, and the Finding That Isn't One
description: The recurring, specific reasons scanners flag things that aren't real barriers — and the more damaging pattern of a fix that makes the scanner happy without touching the actual barrier at all.

learningObjectives.text: Identify common causes of automated false positives
Distinguish a genuine fix from one that satisfies a rule without fixing the barrier

contentSections.title: Why scanners flag things that aren't real

contentSections.body: A scan flags "insufficient colour contrast" on hero text. The text is white, rendered over a photograph, and in the specific area behind the letters the photo is dark enough that the actual contrast is fine — the scanner checked the text colour against the image's *average* colour, not the pixels actually behind the text.

contentSections.scenario: Four scan results, flagged as violations. **A.** "Empty link" on an icon-only social media link that has `aria-label="Follow us on Instagram"` — but the scan ran before the single-page app finished rendering that attribute in. **B.** "Missing form label" on a search input that has a properly associated `<label for>` sitting in a collapsed accordion the scanner didn't expand. **C.** "Duplicate ID" flagged on two elements that are genuinely both `id="nav-item"`, shipped in production. **D.** "Insufficient contrast" on the hero text from the hook above.
contentSections.question: How many of these four are genuine, real defects rather than false positives caused by the tool's own limitations?

options.label: All four
Just C — the duplicate ID is real; the other three are false positives caused by timing, rendering or measurement gaps
None — automated results are unreliable by default

feedback.onlyC: Right. A and B are both real defects the scanner missed because of *timing* — it ran before the SPA finished rendering (A) and didn't interact with the collapsed accordion to reveal the labelled field (B) — meaning the scan actually under-reported, not over-reported, on those two; they're real barriers the automated pass simply never saw, closer to false negatives than false positives. C is a genuine defect: two elements really do share an ID in production, which breaks any `for`/`id` or `aria-labelledby` reference pointing at either one. D is the true false positive: the scanner's algorithm approximated the background colour rather than sampling the actual pixels behind the text, and produced a wrong verdict on an area that's genuinely fine.
feedback.four: This treats every flagged item as automatically correct, which is exactly the over-trust this whole module argues against — one of these four (D) is a measurement artefact, not a real barrier.
feedback.none: The opposite over-correction: dismissing every automated result wastes the roughly one-third of WCAG that genuinely is reliably automatable. C is real and should be fixed without hesitation.

contentSections.concept: **A flagged result can be wrong in either direction, and for different reasons each time**: a genuine false positive (D — the tool's measurement was actually incorrect), a defect the tool missed because of timing or interaction gaps (A, B — arguably worse, since it looks like a clean pass), or a correct flag (C). The discipline this teaches is the same one from the very first module of this track, applied to automated results specifically: **verify before you report, whichever direction the verification points.**

contentSections.code:
Audit finding, drawn directly from an axe scan:

"Serious: Elements must have sufficient color
contrast (WCAG 1.4.3). 1 instance.
Selector: .hero-heading"

[Reported as-is, no further investigation,
severity copied directly from the scanner's label]
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in reporting this finding exactly as the scanner produced it?

options.label: It should also cite 1.4.11 for non-text contrast
The scanner's automated contrast check can be wrong on text over images or gradients — this needs verification against the actual rendered pixels before it's reported as a finding
"Serious" isn't a WCAG-defined severity term

feedback.verify: Correct. Automated contrast checkers commonly sample an approximated background colour rather than the actual pixel behind each character, which produces exactly this kind of false positive on text over images, gradients, or partially transparent overlays. A real audit checks the flagged instance manually — take a screenshot, sample the actual pixel colour behind representative letters, recompute — before it goes in a report a client will act on.
feedback.cite: A second citation doesn't fix the underlying problem, which is that the flagged instance may not even be a real defect yet.
feedback.severity: True as a technicality — "Serious" is the tool's own internal severity label, not a WCAG term — but it's not the actual flaw here. Even correctly re-labelled, an unverified false positive is still a false positive.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Copying a scanner's output directly into a report treats the tool's word as ground truth, which the previous pod just showed isn't always warranted — especially for contrast on any non-solid background, the single most common source of automated false positives in real audits.

contentSections.body: Verify a flagged result before it becomes a finding — in either direction. Some flags are real defects a scan missed the true depth of; some are measurement artefacts on non-solid backgrounds; only checking tells you which.

contentSections.title: The fix that satisfies the rule and not the person

contentSections.body: A developer, under deadline pressure to get a scan to zero, adds `alt="image"` to every unlabelled image on a page. The rule passes. Every one of those images now announces the literal word "image" to a screen reader user — forty times on one product page.

contentSections.scenario: A team is under pressure to bring an axe scan from 23 violations to zero before a release. Judge each fix on whether it addresses the actual barrier or just satisfies the rule's literal check.
contentSections.question: Select every fix below that genuinely addresses the barrier, not just the automated rule.

items.label: Writing a specific, accurate alt description for each of the twelve unlabelled product images
Setting alt="image" on all twelve, to clear the "missing alt attribute" rule
Darkening a button's text colour to genuinely meet 4.5:1 against its background
Adding aria-hidden="true" to the low-contrast text so the scanner stops evaluating it
Associating each form field with a real, descriptive label via for/id
Adding an empty aria-label="" to satisfy the "missing accessible name" rule

explanation.realalt: A genuine fix — a screen reader user now hears what each product actually is, which is the entire point of 1.1.1.
explanation.genericalt: This is the exact failure the hook describes: the rule's literal condition (an alt attribute exists, non-empty) is satisfied, and the user experience is arguably worse than before — forty repetitions of a meaningless word instead of forty repetitions of a filename or a blank.
explanation.realcontrast: A genuine fix — the actual measured ratio now clears the threshold, which is what the criterion is actually asking for.
explanation.hiddencontrast: This removes the element from the accessibility tree entirely rather than fixing its contrast, meaning a screen reader user now can't access that content at all — the scanner stops flagging it because it's stopped checking it, not because the barrier is gone. Sighted users still see the same low-contrast text.
explanation.reallabel: A genuine fix — the field now has a real, usable label a screen reader announces.
explanation.emptylabel: An empty aria-label technically supplies *an* accessible name — the empty string — which some scanners will stop flagging while the field is now announced with no name at all, arguably worse than before the "fix."

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six fix the actual barrier; three satisfy the rule's literal wording while leaving the user experience the same or worse. The pattern across all three bad fixes: each one manipulates what the scanner is checking, rather than the thing the check exists to protect. This is worth watching for specifically under deadline pressure, because "get the scan to zero" is a much easier instruction to satisfy dishonestly than "fix the barriers" is — and a reviewer's job includes catching the difference.

contentSections.body: A scan going to zero can mean the barriers got fixed, or it can mean the rule got gamed. Check which one happened — the difference is invisible to the tool and obvious to the person the fix was supposed to help.

title: Passing the Scan and Failing the User
description: The gap between satisfying a rule's letter and meeting its intent, and how an auditor holds that line when a client's whole case for a shorter engagement rests on a green scan.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the mechanism by which a page passes automated checks and remains genuinely unusable
Respond to pressure to shrink an audit's scope because automated results are clean

contentSections.title: Satisfying the letter, not the intent

contentSections.body: Every image on a page has an alt attribute. Every form field has a label. Contrast passes everywhere. The scan is completely clean. A screen reader user still can't tell which of six identical-looking "Add to cart" buttons belongs to which product, because every one of the six labels reads the literal string "Add to cart" with nothing distinguishing them.

contentSections.scenario: A product listing page has six items, each with an "Add to cart" button. Each button has a correctly associated, non-empty accessible name: "Add to cart." A scan finds zero violations across the whole page.
contentSections.question: Why does this pass every automated check and still fail a screen reader user trying to buy a specific product?

options.label: The scan is misconfigured and should be re-run

Every criterion checkable here (name exists, name is non-empty) is satisfied — distinguishing which button belongs to which product requires understanding the page's layout and content, which no automated rule checks
This isn't actually a real accessibility problem

feedback.uniqueness: Right. Nothing in WCAG's automatable criteria requires that repeated control names be distinguishable from each other in isolation — 4.1.2 asks whether a name exists and is programmatically exposed, and it does, six times over. Whether "Add to cart" uniquely identifies *which* product is a question about relating the control to its surrounding content, which is exactly the kind of contextual judgement no scanner performs. A screen reader user tabbing through hears "Add to cart, button" six identical times with no way to tell them apart without reading back through the whole page.
feedback.misconfig: The scan is very likely working exactly as designed — this is the structural gap this whole module has been building toward, not a configuration error.
feedback.notreal: It's a completely real barrier, and a common one: WCAG 2.5.3's Label in Name and general good practice both point toward unique, descriptive names for repeated controls, even where no single automatable rule catches the specific pattern of six identical labels on one page.

contentSections.mechanism: **Passing every checkable criterion and being usable are related and not identical claims — a page can satisfy the letter of every automatable rule while failing the actual task a user came to do**, when the failure lives in the relationship between elements (this button, in this row, next to this product) rather than in any single element's own properties. This is the sharpest, most concrete version of the very first lesson of this entire track — automated conformance and usability are correlated, not the same thing — and it's worth having one vivid example like this one ready to show a client who's confused about why a green scan and a real complaint can coexist.

contentSections.body: A control can have a technically valid name and still be indistinguishable from five identical ones next to it. Uniqueness-in-context is a relationship, not a property any single automated rule checks.

contentSections.title: Holding the line when the scan is green

contentSections.body: "Our scan's been clean for months — can we cut the manual portion of this audit and just do a quick automated re-check?" This is a completely reasonable question to ask, and the answer to it is the same one this whole module has been building toward.

contentSections.title: The scoping call
contentSections.opening: A returning client's procurement team calls before renewing an audit engagement: "Our automated CI checks have been green for four months straight. Can we scope this year's audit down to just spot-checking the automated results, instead of the full manual pass?"

start.situation: The scan really has been clean — that part is true. The question is what a clean scan actually tells you, and what it doesn't.
start.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Agree — a clean scan for four months is good evidence, cut the manual pass
choices.consequence: This year's audit costs less and finds almost nothing, because it was never designed to find the roughly two-thirds of barrier categories that were never automated in the first place. Six months later, a support ticket describes exactly one of those categories.

choices.label: Refuse to scope it down at all — insist on the full manual pass as originally planned
choices.consequence: Technically the more thorough answer, delivered without engaging the client's actual, reasonable question about where their money is best spent this year.

choices.label: Explain what the scan does and doesn't cover, and propose a scope that keeps manual coverage where it matters most
choices.consequence: You walk through the automated/manual split concretely: the scan reliably catches roughly a third of WCAG's checkable ground, continuously, which is genuinely valuable and worth trusting for that slice. It has never once, and structurally cannot, check task completion, uniqueness of repeated controls, or cognitive load. You propose keeping full manual depth on the three highest-traffic user journeys and trusting the CI gate for routine markup regressions elsewhere.

response.situation: The client asks a fair follow-up: "How do we know the three journeys you pick are the right ones to keep deep?"
response.question: How do you answer that?

choices.label: Base it on actual usage data — the flows the most users actually complete
choices.consequence: The client agrees, scopes this year's engagement to deep manual coverage on the three highest-traffic journeys plus a light automated-results review elsewhere, and gets a defensible, costed answer to a genuinely reasonable question.

agreed.summary: The reduced-scope audit finds almost nothing, not because the product improved, but because it was scoped to only look where automation already looks.
agreed.lesson: A clean scan is real evidence about the automatable third of the standard. Letting it stand in for evidence about the other two-thirds — silently, by cutting the manual pass entirely — produces an audit that confirms what was already known and misses everything it existed to check.

rigid.summary: The full audit gets delivered, at full cost, without ever engaging the client's actual, reasonable budget question.
rigid.lesson: "No" without an alternative treats a legitimate cost question as if it were bad faith. The client's instinct — that a stable CI gate should count for something in how the budget gets allocated — deserved a real answer, not a wall.

resolved.summary: The engagement is scoped honestly: continuous automated coverage trusted for what it actually covers, deep manual review kept exactly where the data says it matters most.
resolved.lesson: The client's question wasn't unreasonable — it just needed the automated/manual boundary explained concretely, with a specific example, rather than either a blanket yes or a blanket no. Naming what the scan can and can't see is what let the actual budget conversation happen on real terms.

contentSections.body: A clean scan is real evidence about the automatable slice of WCAG. Letting it silently stand in for the rest — instead of naming the boundary explicitly — is how a reasonable budget question turns into a genuine coverage gap.

title: Automated Checks in CI: Worth Having, Easy to Over-Trust
description: A CI accessibility gate is genuinely one of the highest-value cheap interventions available — and the exact moment it becomes dangerous is the moment a team stops remembering what it doesn't cover.

learningObjectives.text: State what a CI accessibility gate is good for and what it costs to run
Identify the over-trust failure mode specific to continuous automated checks

contentSections.title: What a CI gate is actually good for

contentSections.body: A team wants to add axe-core to their CI pipeline, failing the build on new violations. It's a genuinely good idea — cheap, fast, and it catches an entire category of regression before it ever reaches a reviewer's desk. The caveat matters just as much as the endorsement.

Wiring axe-core (or a similar rule engine) into CI — via Cypress, Playwright, or a Jest plugin — costs essentially nothing beyond normal CI compute time, since the underlying tool is free and open source. What it buys: every pull request gets checked against the same roughly-third-of-WCAG automatable ruleset, automatically, before a human ever looks at it. A developer who accidentally removes a label, breaks a contrast ratio, or introduces a duplicate ID finds out in minutes, not months later in a client's audit.

This is real, compounding value — regressions caught this early cost almost nothing to fix, exactly the kind of "catch it before it propagates" intervention the earlier module on design-process assumptions was built around.

contentSections.scenario: A team is deciding what to gate merges on. Options under discussion: (1) block any merge that introduces a new axe-core violation; (2) block any merge below a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100; (3) require a full manual screen-reader pass on every PR before merge.
contentSections.question: Which is the sound CI gate?

options.label: Option 1 — block on new automated violations
Option 2 — require a perfect Lighthouse score
Option 3 — require a full manual pass on every PR

feedback.opt1: Right fit for CI. It's fast, deterministic, and scoped honestly to what automation can reliably check — exactly the class of regression this kind of gate exists to catch, with no ambiguity about what "pass" means.
feedback.opt2: A single composite score is a worse gate than a rule-by-rule check: a score can stay at 100 while individual, real defects shift underneath it if the scoring weights don't happen to catch them, and a perfect score requirement invites exactly the rule-gaming this module's third lesson described.
feedback.opt3: Manual review is valuable and completely wrong for a per-PR CI gate — it's slow, requires a human, and would bottleneck every single merge. It belongs in periodic audits and release-level review, not blocking every commit.

contentSections.concept: **A CI gate should check exactly what automation can reliably and deterministically check, and nothing more.** Scoping it honestly — a defined ruleset, pass/fail per rule, no composite score to game — is what keeps it useful. The moment a CI gate starts standing in for the review it was never built to replace is the subject of the next pod.

contentSections.body: A CI accessibility gate is cheap, fast, and genuinely valuable for catching markup-level regressions before they ship. Scope it to exactly what automation reliably checks, and no further.

contentSections.title: The over-trust failure mode, specifically for CI

contentSections.body: Six months into a green CI gate, a team stops mentioning accessibility in planning at all — not because anyone decided it was solved, but because "the check passes" quietly became the entire definition of done, and nobody remembers it was only ever checking a third of the picture.

contentSections.scenario: A team has run a CI accessibility gate cleanly for six months. Judge each statement about what that track record does and doesn't tell them.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that's actually true of a six-month clean CI track record.

items.label: No new markup-level regressions (missing labels, broken IDs, contrast failures) have been introduced in that time
The product is fully usable by disabled users
Every new feature shipped in that window has been checked against the automatable ruleset
Cognitive load and task-completion issues from the module on barriers have not silently accumulated
The gate has probably reduced the frequency of a specific class of defect reaching production
A manual audit would be redundant given this track record

explanation.regressions: True, and it's real, valuable information — the automatable class of defect genuinely has stayed out of production for six months.
explanation.usable: Not something a CI gate can ever tell you, clean track record or not — this is the exact overreach the whole module warns against.
explanation.newcode: True by construction — that's literally what the gate does on every merge.
explanation.cognitive: The gate has never once checked for this, so a clean record says nothing about it either way — it hasn't proven these issues absent, only that nobody's been measuring them.
explanation.confidence: A reasonable, modest inference — worth stating this way rather than as "the product is accessible."
explanation.auditnotneeded: This is the exact reasoning the case-sim in the previous lesson walked through and rejected — a clean automated record is evidence about the automatable third, never a substitute for checking the rest.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six are genuinely supported by a clean CI record; three overreach into territory the gate never measured. The pattern behind the three overreaches: each one silently upgrades "no new automatable defects" into "no new defects, full stop" — which is exactly the drift that happens gradually, over months, without anyone deciding it on purpose.

contentSections.body: A clean CI gate proves the automatable third stayed clean. It's genuinely valuable evidence for exactly that claim, and it's worth restating explicitly — regularly, out loud — that it was never measuring the rest.

title: Practice — Triage Scanner Results
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where telling a real finding from a false positive from an unverifiable claim stops being a lookup.

learningObjectives.text: Triage automated scan results as confirmed, false-positive, or needing verification, at speed
Distinguish a genuine fix from one that only satisfies the automated rule

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing is timed and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Scan a Real Site, Then Find What the Scan Missed
description: Run a real automated scan against a real site, verify what it flagged, and then do the manual pass that finds what it structurally couldn't — the complete picture this module has been building toward.

learningObjectives.text: Run and interpret an automated accessibility scan against a real product
Verify flagged results and identify false positives
Find real barriers a scan structurally could not detect

contentSections.body: A scan report on its own tells you what a machine could check. This lab produces the document that tells the whole story: what the machine found, which of those findings actually hold up, and what a person had to find instead.

contentSections.title: Scan, verify, and go past it
contentSections.brief: Pick a real site or product you can freely explore — something you use, something you're building, or a public site. Run a free automated tool (axe's browser extension, Lighthouse, or WAVE — pick at least one) against two or three of its pages, then do the work this module has been building toward: verify what it found, and manually check for what it structurally could never see.
contentSections.deliverable: A scan report annotated in three parts: confirmed findings (verified real), dismissed findings (false positives, with the reason), and additional findings from manual review that the scan could not have caught.

stages.title: Run the scan
stages.instructions: Run your chosen automated tool against 2-3 pages of the product, covering at least one real user task (not just the homepage). Record the raw results as the tool reports them — don't filter anything yet.
stages.checkpoint: You have a raw, unedited list of automated findings across at least two pages.

stages.title: Verify every flagged result
stages.instructions: For each flagged item, check it directly — inspect the actual markup, sample real contrast where relevant, check the browser's accessibility tree for the computed name. Sort each into confirmed (real, verified) or dismissed (false positive), and for every dismissed one, state the specific reason, the way this module's lessons taught (timing, background image, tool limitation).
stages.checkpoint: Every raw finding is sorted into confirmed or dismissed, with a stated reason for each dismissal.

stages.title: Manually check what the scan structurally couldn't
stages.instructions: Pick one real task on the pages you scanned and complete it keyboard-only, then (if you can) with a screen reader. Specifically look for: repeated controls with indistinguishable names, tab order versus reading order, whether an action's outcome is actually announced, and anything cognitive-load-shaped from the earlier module on barriers.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least one real, manually-found issue the scan did not and structurally could not flag — or, if the task is genuinely clean on manual review too, a clear statement of what you checked and confirmed working.

stages.title: Write the annotated report
stages.instructions: Assemble the three-part document: confirmed automated findings, dismissed findings with reasons, and manual findings — each written the way this track's finding procedure teaches (task, access method, where it stops, what's lost).
stages.checkpoint: All three sections are present, and every finding in any section follows the finding procedure, not just a raw tool output.

rubric.criterion: The scan actually ran against a real task, not just a homepage
rubric.meets: At least one scanned page is part of a real, nameable user task.

rubric.criterion: Every flagged result was actually verified, not assumed
rubric.meets: Confirmed and dismissed findings both show evidence of direct checking, not a copy of the tool's own labels.

rubric.criterion: Dismissals have specific, real reasons
rubric.meets: Every dismissed finding states the actual mechanism (timing, background-image contrast approximation, tool limitation) rather than a vague 'not applicable.'

rubric.criterion: At least one manual finding is present and correctly reasoned
rubric.meets: A real issue the scan structurally could not catch, or a clear confirmation of what was checked and found sound.

rubric.criterion: All findings follow this track's finding procedure
rubric.meets: Task, access method, where it stops, what's lost — not a raw restatement of a tool's summary line.

contentSections.body: The complete picture is never the scan alone and never the manual pass alone. It's the scan, verified, plus what only a person checking by hand can find.

title: Checkpoint — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the previous one, and modules further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's automation-limits content and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find

questions.from: This module — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
questions.prompt: Why is only a minority of WCAG's success criteria fully automatable?

options.label: Today's tools are still immature; future versions will close the gap
Many criteria require understanding meaning or intent, which no static markup analysis can access, at any level of tool sophistication
Tool vendors deliberately limit coverage to sell paid tiers

questions.explanation: The ceiling is structural, not a temporary tooling gap — whether a heading describes its content, whether alt text is accurate, whether tab order matches reading order all require a model of meaning no future scanner version changes.

questions.from: This module — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
questions.prompt: Two scanners disagree sharply on the same page's accessibility. What's the most likely reason?

options.label: One tool is broken
They run different rule subsets at different strictness, presented in different formats — not measuring identically the same thing
The page changed between scans

questions.explanation: Different coverage and presentation choices, not malfunction — Lighthouse's score and axe's full ruleset were never claiming to check the same thing.

questions.from: This module — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
questions.prompt: A scan flags 'insufficient contrast' on text over a photographic background. What's the likely issue?

options.label: The tool approximated the background colour rather than sampling actual pixels — a common false-positive pattern
The finding is definitely real and should be reported as-is
Contrast can never be measured on images

questions.explanation: This is one of the most common automated false positives — verify against the actual rendered pixels before reporting it.

questions.from: This module — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
questions.prompt: A developer sets alt="image" on every unlabelled image to clear a scan. What's the problem?

options.label: None — the rule now passes
The rule's literal condition is satisfied while the actual barrier remains — a screen reader user now hears a meaningless word instead of useful information
It's a violation of a different WCAG criterion

questions.explanation: This is gaming the rule rather than fixing the barrier — the scan goes green while the user experience stays broken or gets worse.

questions.from: This module — What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
questions.prompt: Six identical "Add to cart" buttons on a page, each with a valid, non-empty accessible name, pass every automated check. What do they still fail?

options.label: Nothing — a valid name is sufficient
Distinguishability — a screen reader user can't tell which button belongs to which product, a relationship no single-element rule checks
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, directly

questions.explanation: The gap is in the relationship between elements, not in any single element's own properties — exactly the kind of contextual judgement no automated rule performs.

questions.from: Previous module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: What is a VPAT/ACR?

options.label: An independently audited certification
A self-reported conformance document, often used in procurement, worth verifying against the real product
A legal requirement only outside the US

questions.explanation: Self-reported with no independent verification built in — testing a sample of its claims against the real product is high-leverage work.

questions.from: Previous module — The Law Behind the Standard
questions.prompt: What does a genuine accessibility statement need, beyond a bare conformance claim?

options.label: Nothing more — a conformance level is sufficient
Named specific gaps, a documented burden justification if any content is excluded, a feedback route, and a date
A legal disclaimer only

questions.explanation: A genuine statement names its exceptions specifically and dates itself — "fully accessible" with nothing named is close to always false.

questions.from: Older module — Reading WCAG Properly
questions.prompt: Which layer of WCAG's structure is the one you cite in a finding?

options.label: The principle
The success criterion
The guideline

questions.explanation: Success criteria are the only testable, citable layer — the same discipline this module applied to automated citations.

questions.from: Older module — What Accessibility QA Actually Is
questions.prompt: In the finding procedure, what comes first?

options.label: The citation
The task the user was trying to complete
The severity rating

questions.explanation: Task, access method, where it stops, what they're left with, citation — the same ordering this module used for every scanner finding it wrote up.

questions.from: Older module — How Barriers Get Built
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a barrier and an impairment?

options.label: A barrier is a fact about a design; an impairment is a fact about a body or mind
They're interchangeable
A barrier is a subtype of impairment

questions.explanation: Impairment is a fact about a person. Barrier is a fact about the design. Only the barrier is the reviewer's job to fix.

contentSections.body: This is the end of the Foundations phase. Everything after this builds on these five modules — the phase review pulls from all of them.
